#5436. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5435. Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics

Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.

Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.

Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.

“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.

To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.

That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.

Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.

Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.

To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.

By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.

Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.

“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.

In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.

The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

#5433. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5432. Starburst adds context support to give AI agents consistent access to business data definitions

Starburst Data Inc. is expanding its data federation platform into business context management with the introduction of Context Studio, a new capability designed to help artificial intelligence agents produce more accurate and trustworthy answers from information distributed across enterprise systems.

Context Studio collects business definitions from existing data catalogs, business intelligence tools, metric stores and documents, making them available alongside data when AI agents respond to prompts. The system is intended to eliminate conflicting definitions that can cause AI agents to produce incorrect results.

The new capability addresses a problem the company encountered as customers began deploying its Aida natural-language data assistant in production environments, said Starburst co-founder and Chief Executive Justin Borgman.

“We’ve found that as you get into production, the biggest issue is context because you need to trust the answers the agent gives back,” he said.

The challenge is particularly acute in large organizations where different departments may use different definitions of common business metrics, such as revenue or active customers. Without a consistent understanding of those terms, AI models can produce plausible but inaccurate answers.

“When those definitions conflict, the [large language model] doesn’t know any better; it’s just going to guess,” Borgman said. “That’s what leads to bad answers and an erosion of trust.”

Context Studio builds on Starburst’s existing data products architecture, which allows organizations to create curated views spanning multiple data sources. Those products incorporate business definitions, metadata and access controls that can be applied consistently when agents retrieve information.

Unlike conventional semantic layers that require organizations to consolidate definitions within a single platform, Context Studio federates existing definitions without requiring customers to move or rebuild their underlying data.

Built-in approval workflows resolve conflicting definitions, and a feedback mechanism is provided through which agents can propose improvements. Human reviewers approve changes before regression testing checks their impact on other queries.

Borgman characterized the expansion as an evolution of Starburst’s longstanding strategy of querying distributed data without centralizing it.

“We think context is going to live everywhere, just like we think data will live in multiple places,” he said. “Our approach treats [context] as a first-class principle in our design.”

Starburst hasn’t yet disclosed quantitative evidence of Context Studio’s impact on AI accuracy or productivity. The company said it is collecting benchmark data from private preview customers.

The company is also emphasizing traceability to increase confidence in AI-generated answers. Context Studio records which data sources agents access, the SQL queries they generate and the information used to produce responses. Access controls remain attached to underlying data products.

“Context is going to increase the probability of a good answer, but there’s also a need to trace how it got to that answer,” Borgman said.

An agent can interview domain experts to capture business knowledge and convert it into draft data products. Starburst is also extending its Aida data assistant to answer questions across multiple data products and introducing an agent that automatically generates dashboards.

Other platform enhancements include Mission Control for monitoring usage and costs, automated Apache Iceberg maintenance, a bring-your-own-cloud deployment option and graphics processing unit-accelerated querying. Starburst claims its recently introduced Torin query engine delivers up to sevenfold performance improvements in company benchmarks.

Context Studio is available in private preview for Starburst Galaxy and Starburst Enterprise. A public preview is planned for January, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027. Pricing hasn’t been finalized.

#5431. MetaComp Extends Pre-A+ with Approximately US$10M from Tether and Further

Strategic extension to deepen MetaComp's AsiaâMiddle EastâAfrica payment corridors; proceeds will fund licensing, compliance and payment rails

SINGAPORE, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MetaComp Pte. Ltd. ("MetaComp"), Asia's pioneer in Web2.5 stablecoin/fiat hybrid finance, today announced an extension of its Pre-A+ funding round, with a strategic investment of approximately US$10 million from Tether, the largest company in the digital asset industry, and Further Asset Management ("Further"). The extension brings MetaComp's Pre-A funding round to about US$45 million.

Deepening collaboration on AsiaâMiddle EastâAfrica corridors

Trade between Asia, the Middle East and Africa continues to grow, driving demand for faster and compliant cross-border payments. MetaComp's hybrid fiat and stablecoin infrastructure reduces the intermediaries, settlement delays and fragmented networks that slow traditional cross-border payments on these corridors, reducing settlement from 2-7 days to within 24 hours. With an established client base in Asia, MetaComp supports businesses expanding into markets across Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America, while serving financial institutions and businesses with cross-border payment, wealth management and loan capital raising needs in this region.

Further Asset Management ("Further") is an Abu Dhabi-based global investment platform focused on financial infrastructure and digital assets. Further brings sector expertise and institutional relationships to support MetaComp's growth, including its expansion in the Middle East.

The strategic investment from Tether and Further will accelerate MetaComp's expansion, with proceeds directed towards strengthening its regulatory capabilities, enhancing compliance infrastructure and developing additional payment channels across priority markets.

The extension builds on MetaComp's US$35 million Pre-A and Pre-A+ funding completed in March 2026, backed by investors including Alibaba, Eastern Bell Capital, Noah, Sky9 Capital, and Spark Venture.

Licensed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) as a Major Payment Institution, MetaComp, together with its affiliates[1], provides one-stop financial services from cross-border payments to wealth management.

The platform connects with more than 60 financial institutions and more than 170 payment service providers (PSPs), serves more than 1,000 institutional clients, including leading companies across a wide range of industry verticals, supports 60 currencies across fiat and a range of stablecoins, and processes more than US$1 billion in monthly volume. Assets under management exceed US$600 million. [2]

MetaComp also operates the StableX Agentic Network (SAN), an agentic payment network leveraging stablecoins for AI agents to transact with each other, that is built on SAN's Know-Your-Agent (KYA) compliance standard for network admission and VisionX AI risk intelligence engine for transaction monitoring across fiat and on-chain activities. Since its launch in November 2025, the network has grown to more than 1,000 members reaching more than 100,000 users, with a primary focus on Asia, Middle East, Africa and Latin America.

Dr Bo Bai, Chairman and Co-Founder of MetaComp, said:

"MetaComp has deep roots among companies from Asia, and our network has grown with them as they expand into other parts of Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America. Trade between Asia and the Middle East and Africa is growing fast, and this extension, with Tether and Further, strengthens our capabilities along these corridors. We are building next-generation hybrid financial infrastructure that combines traditional banking rails with stablecoins, giving our clients integrated payment and wealth services in these regions as they expand overseas. The capital will be directed towards licences, compliance and payment channels, the foundations this infrastructure depends on."

Paolo Ardoino, Chief Executive Officer of Tether, said:

"Trade between Asia, the Middle East and Africa is growing fast, but the money behind it still moves too slowly and at too high a cost. Regulated stablecoin infrastructure can change that, and these corridors are exactly where we see potential for USDâ® and XAUâ®. Our investment in MetaComp reflects our focus on building that infrastructure in emerging markets, where faster and cheaper settlement matters most."

Faisal Al Hammadi, Managing Partner at Further Asset Management, said:

"For stablecoins to become everyday financial infrastructure, businesses need reliable connections to the banking systems they already use. MetaComp brings together fiat and stablecoin payment rails, compliance technology and an established institutional client base. That combination fits our investment focus on the infrastructure enabling institutional adoption of digital assets. We look forward to supporting the team's growth and helping it build institutional partnerships across the Middle East."

#5430. XRP Price Prediction: Bears Are Paying to Short XRP, A Short Squeeze?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is struggling to reclaim $1, but its derivatives market is showing an increasingly unusual setup. Traders betting against the token are now paying funding fees to maintain their positions. This creates an interesting possibility for the XRP price prediction. If buying pressure returns, bearish traders could face mounting losses and forced liquidations.

However, the market is not quite ready for a bullish victory lap. Open interest is falling, long positions have already suffered heavy liquidations, and XRP still needs to reclaim important resistance levels.

XRP traded around $0.95, following another difficult session for the crypto market. Meanwhile, its futures market is flashing a rate that dropped in aggregated funding to -0.0068% every eight hours, equivalent to roughly -7.4% annually.

Negative funding means short sellers pay long traders to maintain their perpetual futures positions. In other words, bears are effectively paying a premium to maintain their bearish exposure.

Hyperliquid showed an even more pronounced imbalance, with XRP funding reaching approximately -10.2% annually. The figures suggest bearish positioning has become increasingly expensive across several derivatives markets.

However, there is another side to this trade. XRP open interest declined 5.74% over 24 hours to approximately $1.97 billion, so traders are reducing leverage rather than aggressively opening fresh positions.

While XRP traders debate whether another recovery is coming, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is approaching an important milestone of its own. The Bitcoin Layer 2 project has raised more than $33.2 million during its presale, with its token currently priced at just $0.0136.

The presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving a narrowing window before its anticipated token launch. Buyers choosing the staking option are also being offered an advertised 35% APY during the presale period.

Bitcoin Hyper aims to bring faster Bitcoin transactions and decentralized applications to a new Layer 2 environment. Its architecture combines Solana Virtual Machine execution with zero-knowledge proofs and Bitcoin settlement.

The project has already introduced testnet components, including its explorer, wallet, faucet, and bridge. With the presale approaching its scheduled conclusion, the remaining allocation and upcoming launch milestone could attract additional attention from traders looking beyond established crypto networks.

The immediate question is whether bearish positioning has become sufficiently expensive to trigger an unexpected reversal. A negative funding rate alone cannot confirm a short squeeze. XRP needs to attract fresh spot buyers, recover momentum, and force short sellers to close their positions.

The first important hurdle remains $1.00. Reclaiming this psychological level could encourage sidelined buyers to return and create additional pressure on leveraged shorts.

A sustained move above $1.00 would put $1.10 within reach, followed by a potential test of $1.20 if short liquidations accelerate.

However, the bearish scenario remains firmly in play. Losing the recent $0.89 low could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.80, particularly if Bitcoin continues weakening.

For now, the XRP price prediction hinges on whether negative funding translates into actual buying pressure. Bears are paying longs, but bulls still need to deliver the rally. If they do, the same traders betting against XRP could become the fuel behind its next recovery.

#5429. Another record low for pending home sales, NAR index drops to 63

NAR reported the Pending Home Sales Index fell to 63 in October, down 4.7% from September and 16.7% from a year ago. All 4 regions declined, led by the West, while economists see limited near-term rebound with rates elevated.  AI Summary

Pending home sales fell to yet another record low in October, according to data published by the National Association of Realtors (NAR) on Wednesday.

According to the report, NAR’s Pending Home Sales Index fell to a reading of 63 in October, down 4.7% from a month ago and 16.7% a year ago. An index value of 100 is equivalent to the level of contract signings in 2001.

Despite the new record low, NAR’s chief economist is optimistic that things may turn around in November.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” Yun said in a statement. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s. It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

HousingWire Data, which is more up to date, shows that for the week ending Nov. 13, 2026, 295,621 single family homes were pending in the U.S., down 14.1% from a year ago.

Pending home sales declined in all four major regions on both a year-over-year and month-over-month basis in October, according to NAR data. The West posted both the largest annual and monthly declines, dropping 20.3% from a year ago and 6.9% a month ago to an index value of 45.8. The Northeast (58.5) posted the smallest monthly and annual declines at 0.8% and 11.1%, respectively. Despite falling 18.7% annually and 6.3% from a month ago, pending home sales in the South remained the closest to 2001 levels, with an index reading of 74.5. Meanwhile, pending sales in the Midwest (65.5) fell 2.7% month-over-month and 14.0% from a year ago.

Locally, pending home sells fell annually in all 50 of the largest metro areas analyzed, with the smallest declines occurring inCincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%), Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) and Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) according to data from Realtor.com Economics.

Looking ahead, with the Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates at their meeting in December, economists believe a near-term rebound in contract signings is unlikely.

“A meaningful rebound looks unlikely any time soon, with further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve likely to keep a floor under rates as it keeps up its fight against inflation,” Sam Williamson, First American’s senior economist, said in a statement. “While those hikes could eventually open the door to lower rates, but it will take convincing evidence that inflation is retreating toward the Fed’s target. In the meantime, life events will keep some households moving, even as high rates discourage move-up and other discretionary moves and give some first-time buyers a little more reason to wait. Higher incomes and slower price growth may restore some buying power, but rates will limit how much of it turns into sales.”

#5428. Linq Raises $90 Million in New Funding Led by Andreessen Horowitz to Build the Infrastructure Platform for AI Agents

Every business and every person will have an agent. With more than 1 billion messages processed, Linq is building the infrastructure to put them to work.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Linq, the infrastructure platform for AI agents, today announced $90 million in new funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, with continued participation from TQ Ventures, Mucker Capital, and Abstract, and new participation from Anthos and Left Lane Capital. Ben Horowitz will join its board of directors.

The internet gave every business a website. The iPhone gave every business an app. Now AI is giving every business, and every person, an agent. Cloudflare reports that more than half of internet traffic is no longer human, with AI agent requests on its network up more than 1,700% in a year. These are not simple, customer-service chatbots: these agents book, buy, and make plans by communicating with people and using software on their behalf.

Messaging was Linq's first product and remains a core part of its growing AI infrastructure platform. As the provider for DoorDash, Town, Tomo, and hundreds of others, Linq has already processed more than 1 billion messages. DoorDash uses Linq to help customers find food, build a cart, and check out in a single thread. And now, as an Apple Messaging Service Provider, Linq can help more enterprises launch and scale customer-facing agents on the same channel.

"The best AI experiences fit naturally into people's lives," said Aryan Shah, Head of AI research at DoorDash. "Linq gives us the messaging infrastructure to bring ordering into a familiar conversation, so customers can go from deciding what they want to placing an order in one thread."

"Agents will communicate and get work done just like people do. Linq gives agents the infrastructure to do both at scale," said Ben Horowitz, cofounder and general partner at Andreessen Horowitz.

Messaging is the beginning of a larger shift: people will describe what they need, and agents will get it done. Linq's computer use offering gives agents access to physical computing infrastructure to interact with software and complete tasks. HD Calling for Agents adds voice calling to the platform. The funding will support continued investment in messaging and the expansion of Linq's product lineup through its own software, hardware infrastructure, and strategic partnerships.

"Clicking through five screens to make a payment will become two words to an agent: 'pay rent,'" said Elliott Potter, CEO of Linq. "We help developers build customer-facing agents that use human tools to do human work."

Companies can learn more at https://linqapp.com/

Linq is the platform for building AI agents. It brings together messaging and an expanding set of tools for interacting with the world, helping developers spend less time assembling infrastructure and more time building products. Learn more at https://linqapp.com/

#5427. AI and supercomputing merge as universities build GPU clusters at cloud-provider scale

Universities racing to build AI infrastructure are learning that raw compute changes the pace of science itself, from molecular discovery to materials engineering.

AI and high-performance computing are converging, and campus technology leaders are now building like cloud operators. The Texas A&M University System is standing up two major clusters for researchers across its 12 universities and eight state agencies, according to Vince Kellen (pictured), chief information officer of The Texas A&M University System.

“A lot of it is going to be related to molecules, molecular discovery, and the size of these computers lets researchers go through their research program in a fraction of the time. What would normally take five months now gets done in a week,” Kellen said. “That’s a big deal for the scientists. It lets them do more exploration more frequently.”

Kellen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the system’s supercomputing clusters are speeding up molecular discovery, the security and operational demands of running them, and the convergence of AI and supercomputing. (* Disclosure below.)

The system’s VISION supercomputer, an Nvidia Corp. DGX H200 SuperPOD, ranked No. 66 on the June 2026 Top500 list, making it the most powerful university supercomputer in the U.S. — with a second cluster on the way, according to Kellen. The Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station selected Dell Technologies Inc. to build IGNITE, a platform running Advanced Micro Devices Inc. GPUs in an Equinix Inc. data center in Dallas. With some research tied to highly secure federal contracts, protection tops the policy agenda.

“On the policy side, our main concern is security. Are we doing this in a secure way?” Kellen said. “Are we vetting the employees who are coming into the platform to make sure that they’re properly credentialed to come in?”

Texas A&M is working through those access questions as it brings more computing power to researchers across the system, but faster molecular discovery is only the first payoff. Materials engineering, fluid dynamics and other engineering disciplines are next in line, and the system has no plans to slow its buildout, according to Kellen.

“We already know that AI and supercomputing are one and the same,” he said. “That trajectory is going to continue in Texas for some time.”

#5426. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5425. The mortgage industry was built to help Americans buy homes. An aging America needs more from it.

Survey of 2,000 homeowners 55 plus shows 88% prioritize staying home and 90% prioritize independence

For decades, the mortgage industry has helped Americans achieve one of their biggest financial goals: buying a home and building equity over time.

It’s a model we know well. Homeowners purchase properties, make mortgage payments, refinance when it makes financial sense and gradually accumulate wealth. Much of the mortgage industry is structured around supporting that journey.

But what happens after decades of building that wealth?

As homeowners approach retirement, the financial equation shifts. Instead of focusing primarily on acquiring a home and paying down debt, the question becomes how to use the wealth they’ve accumulated to support the years ahead. Housing presents a unique opportunity but also a challenge because, for many Americans, their largest financial asset is also the place they call home.

You can sell a stock without moving. Selling a home is another matter. Trading down and moving to a less expensive home to tap home equity is both expensive and difficult. This might be why our recent research shows that the desire to remain at home continues to grow stronger with age.

In a recent Longbridge Financial, LLC (NMLS #957935) study of more than 2,000 U.S. homeowners ages 55 and older, 90% said maintaining their independence was extremely or very important to their ideal retirement. Nearly as many (88%) said the same about remaining in their homes. Both priorities ranked above paying for health care, paying off debt, long-term care and providing financial support to family members.

The desire to age in place isn’t surprising. What’s particularly revealing is how strongly that sentiment differs across age groups.

Among homeowners ages 55 to 64, 85% rated remaining in their homes as extremely or very important. That figure rose to 88% among those ages 65 to 74 and 93% among homeowners 75 and older. The importance of maintaining independence followed a similar pattern, climbing from 87% in the youngest group to 96% in the oldest.

These are differences between age groups at one point in time, rather than a measure of how individual preferences change over time. Still, the pattern points to an important finding in understanding how homeowners think about retirement.

Over decades, homeowners accumulate substantial equity through mortgage payments and increases in property values. Yet the very home that holds the wealth is also where many want to spend their later years. Its financial value tells only part of the story. Giving a homeowner a choice to move to a less expensive, and thus less attractive, home to use their home equity may not be much of a choice at all.

Consider two retired households with the same net worth. One holds most of its wealth in savings and investments. The other holds much of it in home equity.

Their balance sheets might look similar, but their financial flexibility is different. The first household may be able to draw from liquid accounts to cover an unexpected expense. The second has wealth, too, but accessing it may involve borrowing against the home or selling it altogether. Both options come with trade-offs, particularly when remaining in the home is a priority.

For an industry accustomed to measuring property values, loan balances and equity, this is an important distinction. These figures describe a homeowner’s financial position, but not necessarily how easily they can access that wealth — or what they might have to give up in the process.

The same survey reinforces why this distinction matters. Among homeowners ages 55 to 64, 73% rated paying for health care as extremely or very important to their ideal retirement. That figure climbed to 85% among those 75 and older. While these findings don’t tell us how much homeowners will spend or whether they’ll tap into their home equity, they do highlight how financial priorities can shift across different stages of life.

Mortgage finance has traditionally centered on transactions: purchasing, refinancing, servicing and eventually paying off a loan. Those functions remain essential. But paying off a mortgage doesn’t end a homeowner’s financial relationship with their home.

For some older homeowners, selling or downsizing may be the right choice. Others may have sufficient income and savings to remain in place. Still others may consider home equity loans, lines of credit or reverse mortgages, depending on their financial circumstances, eligibility and the associated costs and risks.

The opportunity for our industry extends beyond any single product. It’s about understanding the role home equity can play in supporting homeowners through retirement, while recognizing the personal value they place on remaining in their homes.

It also requires recognizing that homeowners’ priorities differ. In our study, 93% of women rated independence as extremely or very important, compared with 88% of men. Similar five-point gaps appeared for remaining at home and paying for health care. While the research doesn’t explain why these differences exist, it underscores the importance of understanding homeowners as individuals rather than treating homeowners 55 and over as a single market with identical needs and priorities.

Housing has always been both an investment and a place to live. As homeowners age, the balance between those roles deserves greater attention from the industry that helped them achieve homeownership in the first place.

We’ve spent decades helping Americans build wealth through homeownership. The next opportunity is helping them understand how that wealth can support the years ahead, without losing sight of what they value most: independence, financial flexibility and, for many, the ability to remain at home.

#5424. JOYY Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results: Total revenues record consistent increases, driven by sustained growth of three core businesses

SINGAPORE, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- JOYY Inc. (NASDAQ: JOYY) ("JOYY" or the "Company"), a leading global technology company, today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

In the third quarter, JOYY maintained solid growth momentum. Total revenues reached US$624.6 million, up 15.6% year over year and 5.7% quarter over quarter. Social entertainment revenue was US$441.0 million, up 8.8% year over year. BIGO Ads, including both first-party and third-party businesses, generated US$145.7 million in revenue, up 39.6% year over year, with its third-party advertising business sustaining strong growth of 52.3% year over year. SHOPLINE revenue reached US$37.8 million, up 24.7% year over year. The contribution from non-livestreaming revenue further increased to 32.8% of total revenues this quarter, driven by the Company's multi-engine growth strategy.

JOYY's non-GAAP operating income reached US$46.6 million, up 14.6% year over year. Non-GAAP EBITDA reached US$55.7 million, up 10.1% year over year. Operating cash inflow for the quarter was US$102.2 million. As of September 30, 2026, JOYY held US$2.94 billion in net cash. Supported by the Company's strong cash flow generation and solid financial position, it continued to return capital to its shareholders for their long-term support through cash dividends and share repurchases. As of November 13, the Company has returned a total of US$536.0 million to shareholders this year.

Ms. Ting Li, Chairperson and Chief Executive Officer of JOYY, commented, "We have continued to execute our multi-engine growth strategy, strengthening our core Social Entertainment business while developing Ad Tech and Smart Commerce as two new growth engines. Following our investments and business model validation over the past few years, the results of this strategy are becoming increasingly evident in sustained topline expansion. Looking ahead to 2027, we believe JOYY will enter an important phase as we advance our multi-engine growth strategy and translate our progress into stronger operating results. With increasingly clear growth paths across our three businesses, we are confident in the Company's ability to sustain solid revenue growth in 2027. We also expect greater scale, a stronger earnings mix, and improved operating efficiency to drive further growth in operating profitability."

In the third quarter, Social Entertainment continued to deliver steady growth, with year-over-year growth momentum further accelerating. The Company's global average mobile MAUs reached 278.8 million, up 4.7% year over year. Livestreaming revenue reached US$419.8 million, up 8.1% year over year and 4.3% quarter over quarter. Driven by effective and refined operations, the number of core livestreaming paying users grew 8.1% year over year and 4.8% quarter over quarter.

Bigo Live, the Company's flagship product, continued its steady revenue growth, supported by ongoing improvements in content operations, its streamer ecosystem, and AI applications. In content operations, Bigo Live continued to build on its strengths as a global social platform to better cater to users' cross-regional content consumption and social interaction needs. Bigo Live further refined its cross-regional content distribution algorithms, expanded live translation coverage, and enhanced speech recognition in complex acoustic environments, making it easier for cross-language communication. These improvements drove continued growth in cross-regional gifting among users in developed markets. In terms of the streamer ecosystem, Bigo Live continued to invest in its community by refining growth and incentive mechanisms for new streamers. In particular, Bigo Live improved onboarding and guidance to help newly signed streamers successfully launch their first livestreams. These efforts contributed to a 4.7-percentage-point increase in the share of newly signed streamers completing their first livestream compared with the previous quarter, bolstering Bigo Live's high-quality content pipeline. Bigo Live continued to integrate AI into livestream interactions and virtual gifting, expanding its AI-generated interactive content and virtual gifts to create a more personalized experience for users. In September, the share of total virtual gift consumption attributable to AI-generated interactive virtual gifts increased further to 35.4%.

Furthermore, Bigo Live continued to deepen local community engagement and foster vibrant creator ecosystems. In the Middle East and North Africa, as an official content partner of the 2026 Esports World Cup, Bigo Live delivered an immersive viewing format that integrated tournament livestreams with interactive experiences. Across Southeast Asia, Bigo Live hosted multiple mid-year galas in local markets, supporting the growth of local creators and the sustainable development of its ecosystem. In North America, BIGO Academy combined online growth challenges with offline recognition, highlighting the vitality of its creator ecosystem and strong user engagement. In South America, Bigo Live held its inaugural offline event in Brazil and organized roadshows in Colombia and Peru, expanding public awareness of the platform and fostering a more vibrant and inclusive local creator ecosystem.

In the third quarter, BIGO Ads continued to expand its global traffic network, diversify its advertiser verticals and demand mix, while improving its algorithms and ad delivery efficiency. As a result, BIGO Ads' revenue reached US$145.7 million, up 39.6% year over year and 9.0% quarter over quarter. Its third-party advertising business, BIGO Audience Network, grew 52.3% year over year and 9.2% quarter over quarter.

On the supply side, BIGO Ads continued to expand its global developer ecosystem and broaden the high-quality traffic coverage. In the third quarter, SDK traffic grew 55.6% year over year. In October, BIGO Ads SDK became generally available via Google AdMobâ¢ Mediation as an in-app bidding partner. Developers can now seamlessly access the BIGO Ads SDK through Google AdMob Mediation and tap into massive demand from global premium advertisers. This integration creates new opportunities for BIGO Ads to expand its premium traffic supply and reach a broader range of app categories.

On the demand side, BIGO Ads continued to strengthen its presence in key verticals by expanding its local advertiser base and accumulating more advertiser conversion data. These insights helped further refine its algorithms and optimize ad delivery solutions across different web-based verticals. Web-based advertising demand continued to accelerate, growing by approximately 328% year over year and 30% quarter over quarter, becoming a key driver of BIGO Ads' growth this quarter. Meanwhile, in-app demand maintained healthy growth momentum.

On the technology side, BIGO Ads continued to enhance its data and AI-driven algorithm capabilities to improve the precision and efficiency of ad delivery. As its cross-channel attribution systems improved and advertiser conversion data accumulated, the platform further upgraded its model architecture to support multiple conversion objectives and types of traffic, improving algorithm accuracy and iteration efficiency. Meanwhile, BIGO Ads continued to refine its bidding strategies to better assess the value of each ad impression and match advertiser budgets with available inventory more effectively. These improvements helped advertisers meet their ROI targets while enhancing the efficiency of BIGO Ads' traffic acquisition and monetization.

In the third quarter, SHOPLINE continued to focus on acquiring high-quality brand merchants, strengthening its presence in key markets, and enhancing its omnichannel commerce infrastructure and value-added services. SHOPLINE's revenue reached US$37.8 million, up 24.7% year over year and 10.0% quarter over quarter.

In the cross-border business, SHOPLINE enhanced its service offerings and local support to help these merchants migrate to its platform, manage operations across markets, and process cross-border transactions more efficiently. In the third quarter, revenue from cross-border merchants maintained strong momentum, growing 77.8% year over year. To support the growing base of brand merchants, the Company continued to enhance SHOPLINE Payments with more local payment options, stronger multi-currency payment support, and improved transaction management. These enhancements helped merchants manage cross-border payments easily and efficiently.

In AI Commerce, SHOPLINE's strategy revolves around helping merchants capture demand from AI channels and improve their operational efficiency. As AI agents change how consumers discover and purchase products, SHOPLINE continued to strengthen its capabilities and expand integrations with the broader AI ecosystem. While volume from AI channels is still in an early stage, adoption is building quickly. In the third quarter, page views and order volume from AI channels grew nearly 500% and 550% year over year, respectively. Notably, AI is demonstrating distinct advantages in categories such as consumer electronics and furniture, where shoppers weigh multiple options before buying. In these categories, AI can better interpret consumer needs, recommend relevant products, and guide shoppers toward a purchase. SHOPLINE Omi, an AI-powered commerce assistant, has rolled out features spanning product management, customer segmentation, promotional events, guidance on platform features and settings, and detailed store performance analysis, bringing AI deeper into merchants' day-to-day workflows and improving operational efficiency.

#5423. How far can brokerages go when clawing back commissions from departing agents?

The Q2 2026 Agent Migration Report found external brokerage switches essentially unchanged year over year. In Massachusetts, Lamacchia Realty alleges Chinatti Realty imposed 75%-85% referral fees tied to database leads, and the court cited missing CRM records during discovery.  AI Summary

The number of real estate agents moving from one brokerage brand to another essentially remained flat year-over-year during the second quarter of 2026, according to the Q2 2026 Agent Migration Report, published by Recruiting Insight and Lone Wolf Technologies in late July.

Of the 113,372 records and four MLS corridors the report analyzed, just 3,390 agents made an external move during the quarter, a difference of just six moves from Q2 2025.

At the same time, the report found that name-brand internal transfers grew from 526 in Q4 2024 to 800 in Q2 2026, a 52% increase over 18 months.

While agents may choose to change firms for access to better technology and educational opportunities or to be working in a company culture that better aligns with their values, these moves do not happen in a vacuum and can have real financial consequences for agents.

Some firms have been known to employ “clawbacks,” where the brokerage firm may withhold a percentage of pending commissions on listings nearing contract, charge transfer or cancellation fees if clients follow the agent, or “claw back” signing bonuses or incentives the agents have received upon changing firms.

A lawsuit in Massachusetts, however, claims that one brokerage has taken things a step further, charging referral fees as high as 85% when an agent who left the company closed a transaction with a lead that exists in their former brokerage’s database.

In a suit originally filed in August 2024 and amended in late February 2025, Lamacchia Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, eight of its agents and its former sales manager Jason Posnick, claim that Chinatti Realty Group and its broker-owner Lisa Chinatti has been unjustly enriched through her referral fee practices.

The lawsuit, first reported by Inman, is pending in Massachusetts Superior Court for Middlesex County. It claims that the agent plaintiffs’ independent contractor agreements were unconscionable because they imposed referral fees as high as 85% when they closed transactions with leads in the Chinatti Realty Group’s database after joining Lamacchia Realty.

The agent plaintiffs allege that this allowed Chinatti and her firm to continually make claims for referral fees on many of the agents’ sales since they have left the company and that this has prevented them from earning a living in real estate. Lamacchia Realty claims that, to date, it has paid Chinatti Realty Group in excess of $350,000 in 75% to 85% referral fees on behalf of former Chinatti agents.

In addition to this, the agents claim that they were not paid anything on transactions that were pending when they transitioned from Chinatti to Lamacchia. Lamacchia Realty has said it has paid agents $113,443 to make them whole on commissions not paid to them from Chinatti for pending transactions that closed after they departed Chinatti Realty Group.

The agents also claim Chinatti and her firm misclassified them as independent contractors despite exercising controls beyond the normal supervisory obligations of a broker.

Lamacchia Realty first contacted Chinatti and her firm regarding these alleged issues in November of 2022 via letter.

This past summer, during the discovery process, the court and Judge Lynn Rooney, who is overseeing the suit, said they learned that Chinatti Realty Group had swapped consumer relationship management software providers from Real Geeks to Zillow’s Follow Up Boss in December 2024. To move the data over, Chinatti said Zillow paid a vendor to handle the migration, but that the vendor found certain records were unable to be transferred.

According to a mid-September ruling from the court, Chinatti knew the allegedly lost records were relevant to the dispute between the firms thanks to the November 2022 letter she and her firm received from Lamacchia.

“I find that Lisa Chinatti knew when she received the demand letter in November 2022 that the information contained in Real Geeks was highly relevant to the plaintiffs’ causes of action. I find that Lisa Chinatti did nothing to preserve that documentation and instead, deliberately and intentionally caused the Real Geeks CRM to be destroyed,” Judge Rooney wrote in her ruling. “I find that the Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they have suffered unfair prejudice as a result of Ms. Chinatti’s actions. Plaintiffs likely would have retained the services of a forensic expert to review the data contained in Real Geeks. As stated at the hearing, the Real Geeks data would have included information concerning the daily work and activity of each of the plaintiff agents, statements by Ms. Chinatti, and the nature of the interactions/communications between Ms. Chinatti and the plaintiff agents.”

If the lawsuit proceeds to trial, the judge has said that at a minimum, the plaintiffs were entitled to “very clear and forceful instruction [to the jury] that the evidence, had it been available, would have been unfavorable to the Defendants.”

In addition to this, the court said it discovered that agents’ CRM activity and phone conversations were monitored and recorded, without the permission of call participants. The judge said she had forwarded the ruling and these concerns to the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Criminal Bureau for review of potential wiretap violations.

Earlier this month, the plaintiffs filed a motion for the denial of the summary judgement motions the defendants have filed since the start of the year. They argue that the unresolved factual disputes that have surfaced during discovery warrant a trial and have requested that the court schedule a final pretrial conference.

The court has yet to rule on this motion or Chinatti’s motions for summary judgement.

Chinatti did not respond to HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the allegations in the lawsuit nor the court’s ruling.

#5422. /C O R R E C T I O N - Frost & Sullivan/

In the news release, ISDN Holdings Limited Receives Frost & Sullivan's 2026 Asia-Pacific Customer Value Leadership Recognition for Integrated Industrial Automation Intelligence Leadership, issued 17-Nov-2026 by Frost & Sullivan over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

ISDN Holdings Limited is recognized for combining full-stack industrial automation capabilities, application-focused engineering, and customer-centric innovation to deliver measurable value across APAC.

SAN ANTONIO, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Frost & Sullivan is pleased to announce that ISDN Holdings Limited (ISDN) has received the 2026 Asia-Pacific Customer Value Leadership Recognition in the integrated industrial automation intelligence industry for its strong customer-centric strategy, engineering expertise, and ability to deliver integrated automation solutions across diverse industrial environments. The recognition highlights ISDN's sustained focus on solving complex customer requirements through technology-agnostic integration, localized engineering support, and lifecycle service capabilities.

Frost & Sullivan evaluates companies through a rigorous benchmarking process across two core dimensions: business impact and customer impact. ISDN demonstrated strength across both dimensions by aligning its technology capabilities with evolving industrial requirements while executing solutions with agility across the Asia-Pacific region.

"ISDN combines deep engineering expertise and broad technology capabilities with the agility, responsiveness, and customer focus needed to solve complex automation challenges across Asia's diverse industrial landscape. This unique combination creates a differentiated market position," said Arun Prasath, Principal Consultant at Frost & Sullivan.

Founded in 1986 and headquartered in Singapore, ISDN has developed into a full-stack industrial automation company serving more than 10,000 customers through approximately 75 offices across Asia. Its capabilities span motion control, system solutions, precision manufacturing, software, and renewable energy, supporting sectors including semiconductors, Industry 4.0 manufacturing, medical devices, industrial robotics, aerospace, and clean energy.

ISDN's technology-agnostic approach and broad ecosystem of global technology partners enable it to combine components and technologies into application-specific solutions while providing localized engineering expertise. Its capabilities extend across motion control, edge-to-cloud integration, industrial connectivity, machine analytics, IIoT, cloud and edge computing, and intelligent manufacturing.

Innovation remains central to ISDN's customer value proposition. The company has expanded its capabilities up the automation stack through in-house software, AI-enabled industrial tools, and turnkey solutions. Its AI-powered industrial alarm management solution, for example, collects signals from intelligent sensors, devices, controllers, and IIoT systems, prioritizes alerts, and assigns tasks to relevant personnel through existing communication platforms. Deployments across an oil company in Thailand, a semiconductor manufacturing facility in Singapore, and a Singapore data center demonstrate its application-focused approach.

"For the past 40 years, ISDN and our subsidiaries have worked quietly behind the scenes of industrial automation, making technologies work together and keeping our customers' operations moving. This recognition brings that collective contribution into focus. Our strength lies in understanding each customer's challenges and combining engineering expertise, technology and local support to deliver practical results. As we expand into AI-enabled automation, our purpose remains the same: to improve productivity, strengthen operational reliability and help customers adapt to changing demands. We thank our customers, technology partners and teams across Asia for making this possible." - Mr. Teo Cher Koon, President, and Managing Director of ISDN Holdings Limited

ISDN's customer-first model is reinforced by its full-stack engineering capabilities and modular organizational structure. By combining in-house engineering, precision manufacturing, software development, system integration, and a regional partner ecosystem, the company can customize solutions while addressing requirements across the asset lifecycle. Its smart warehouse solution, developed with Schneider Electric, has delivered a 50% productivity gain, a 91% reduction in stocktaking time, and a 33% decrease in manpower.

"ISDN's high retention among top accounts reflects a consistent track record of application-accurate solutioning. The company engages with customers at the requirements stage to understand their needs and deliver desired outcomes. This discipline, sustained over 40 years and now extended to AI-enabled tools, underpins its customer satisfaction metrics and competitive positioning," said Iqra Azam, Best Practices Research Analyst at Frost & Sullivan.

Frost & Sullivan commends ISDN for establishing a differentiated model that combines technical depth, application-specific customization, regional responsiveness, and sustained customer engagement. Its continued expansion into high-growth areas including semiconductors, data centers, intelligent factories, energy storage, renewable energy, and physical AI further reflects its focus on evolving industrial requirements.

#5421. OneTrust’s Fall ’26 Release expands AI visibility, privacy and third-party risk tools

Governance platform provider OneTrust LLC today announced its Fall ’26 Release, a set of platform updates said to bring governance into the workflows where business decisions are made.

Leading the list of updates is a revised AI inventory, which is designed to reflect changes across a customer’s environment on a continuous basis. According to OneTrust, the change is needed because many organizations running complex networks of AI systems and agents have only limited visibility into how those systems operate. Model associations, potential matches and deprecation indicators from providers are now pulled into the inventory from a curated library of foundation models.

Relationships among AI systems, models, agents, projects, risks, controls and workflows can be explored through an interactive AI lineage view. AI performance and operational dashboards, added in the release, bring usage, associated risk, evaluation coverage, outbound personally identifiable information discovery and token consumption into one summary.

On the third-party risk side, a workflow rule that launches a risk assessment can now trigger OneTrust’s Deep Research AI skill. The in-depth research report that the skill compiles from public data sources is then used to answer the assessment questionnaire. OneTrust claims the integration can cut the time needed to complete a third-party risk assessment from weeks to minutes.

Drawing on previous assessments and supplier documentation, the company’s expanded AI Document Scanning and Inventory Response Analysis features can now also answer questions about the business engagement tied to a third party.

In the company’s consent management platform, navigation, configuration, scanning, publishing and geolocation management have also been brought into a single workflow under a modernized interface.

OneTrust is sharing availability details for the Fall ’26 Release through an overview webinar.

OneTrust has raised $1.13 billion to date, including $150 million in 2023 at a valuation of $4.5 billion. Investors in the company include Insight Partners LP, Coatue Management, Technology Crossover Ventures LP, SoftBank Vision Fund 2 LP, Franklin Resources Inc., Generation Investment Management LLP and Sands Capital Management.

#5420. Real REMAX Group confirms additional layoffs after merger

Real REMAX Group confirmed additional organizational changes after its REMAX acquisition. Executives previously disclosed a 14% headcount reduction and more than $40 million in annualized gross cost savings tied to integration efforts.  AI Summary

After a merger or acquisition closes, companies almost always look for cost synergies. These efforts frequently result in layoffs, which they did at the recently formed Real REMAX Group, a RealTrends Verified firm.

During the company’s third-quarter 2026 earnings call with investors and analysts, which occurred a little over two months after The Real Brokerage closed its acquisition of REMAX, executives said the company reduced its combined headcount by more than 14%, eliminating 150-plus positions across the combined organization.

This came as the company said it found more than $40 million in annualized gross cost savings and expects to realize more than $30 million in adjusted EBITDA savings in 2027, which could increase to more than $40 million in 2028.

At the time of the earnings call, executives said the initial phase of headcount restructuring was largely complete but that they were still looking for ways to simplify operations and improve efficiencies.

But based on a recent slew of posts on LinkedIn, it appears that headcount reductions are not over just yet. Over the past week, several individuals who claim to be former REMAX employees shared posts stating that they’d been impacted by a recent round of layoffs at the company.

A spokesperson for Real REMAX Group told HousingWire via email that following the acquisition, “Real REMAX Group is continuing to evaluate opportunities that streamline operations, create efficiencies and better integrate the two organizations.”

“As part of this ongoing process, we can confirm that additional organizational changes have taken place at the company,” the spokesperson wrote. “We will continue to assess our business needs to ensure we have the right structure and resources in place to support our long-term strategic priorities and better serve real estate professionals.”

The spokesperson declined to share details regarding the size of the layoffs, which departments were impacted or if the layoffs were performance related.

Real REMAX Group is not alone in laying off employees as part of an attempt to rightsize after a merger.

Earlier this year, Compass International Holdings announced it was laying off 110 employees after it closed its acquisition of Anywhere Real Estate. Compass has estimated $500 million in total net cost synergies over the next three years.
