#5418. Tesorai raises $5.3M to feed starving AI models with biological data and accelerate drug discovery

Drug researchers and medical laboratories generate massive volumes of biological data every single day, yet somehow the artificial intelligence models designed to speed up drug discovery are still starved of useful information.

It’s a strange paradox, but a startup called Tesorai Inc. believes it has the solution after raising $5.3 million in seed funding today.

The round included Perplexity Fund, IQT, South Central Ventures, New Stack Ventures, NextGen Venture Partners, f7 Ventures, VitalStage Ventures and ZAKA participating. With its completion, Tesorai has now raised $8 million in total, and will use that money to try to accelerate AI-driven scientific discovery by digging deeper into existing datasets to surface the deeply buried insights that human researchers have missed.

Biological data covers a broad spectrum spanning genetic sequences to protein measurements, and metabolomic processes to cellular imaging. This information is extremely valuable to drug researchers, because it serves as the primary fuel for training advanced AI models that can predict disease pathways and identify new therapies.

AI-accelerated drug discovery is seen as one of the most promising use cases for this technology, but it hasn’t yet managed to change the world in the same way that generative AI has done. Why not? Because researchers still don’t have nearly enough of it, which limits the accuracy of the best models they’ve come up with so far.

To combat this scarcity of biological data, tech giants including OpenAI Group PBC, Google LLC’s DeepMind, Meta Platforms Inc., Isomorphic Labs Inc. and others are spending billions of dollars to generate more of it, but Tesorai’s co-founders Charlie Kim, Melissa Miao and Peter Cimermancic believe it’s also possible to do more with less.

To that end, Tesorai’s goal is to unlock the biological data that researchers already have access to. Rather than using the summarized findings available in published research papers and clinical studies, it uses AI to analyze raw spectrometry data generated by lab instruments.

Its platform consists of Tesorai Search, which rapidly ingests and analyzes terabytes of data from different sources. There’s also Tesorai Chat, which is used by scientists to ask questions of biological datasets in plain English. And there’s Tesorai Trove, a curated catalog of thousands of publicly available datasets and studies.

Those three components work together to process the raw instrument data from both new and historical lab studies and experiments, before analyzing it thoroughly to try to surface insights that were missed by their authors. By using those insights, Tesorai believes it can train more accurate AI models for drug discovery and therapy research.

“Life science R&D is accelerating and becoming increasingly autonomous, which makes it more important to extract as much insight as possible from every experiment,” Chief Scientific Officer Kim explained. “Tesorai does this for a lab’s new data and for thousands of published studies, and the gains compound as each experiment builds on the last. Ultimately, this will help the industry to develop better medicines faster.”

The startup points to a number of discoveries it has unearthed that were missed by previous studies. In one example, Tesorai reprocessed and re-crunched the data from five studies of the human brain in Alzheimer’s disease-afflicted patients. Through its analysis, it identified a key Alzheimer’s biomarker called p-tau217 that was missed in all five of the studies. Tesorai ran the analysis to test an Alzheimer’s blood panel published in JAMA Neurology in August, and it posted its findings as a preprint later that month.

In another example, Tesorai illustrated how it was able to accelerate AI model training by adding protein data to a small single-cell AI model, enabling it to beat larger RNA-only models, including one with 40 times more parameters, on multiple benchmarks.

Miao, who’s Tesorai’s chief executive officer, said basically every scientific study produces much more data than what’s reported by its authors. Moreover, most of those studies are never revisited. “Our platform reclaims the value of experiments that have already been done and amplifies each new experiment with the relevant evidence that already exists,” she said.

Tesorai’s early success has paved the way for its initial traction, and it has already established partnerships with the MD Anderson Cancer Center, New York University and the Michael J. Fox Foundation. With the funds from today’s round, it will try to secure more partnerships with the life sciences industry, catalog more public studies and expand its platform to cover other molecular data beyond proteins and genomes.

Perplexity Fund General Partner Joanna Lee Shevelenko said it’s clear that AI can dramatically accelerate scientific research, and that’s why it needs as much high-quality experimental data as possible. “Tesorai is building the infrastructure to make that data usable at scale, giving scientists and AI systems a stronger foundation for advancing research,” she said.

#5417. Guild’s Nora Guerra on helping baby boomers buy and rehab homes with reverse mortgages

Guild Mortgage’s Nora Guerra said lenders underserve older, equity-rich buyers despite NAR data showing boomers are 42% of buyers and 55% of sellers. She pointed to $15.34 trillion in 62-plus housing wealth and rising use cases for reverse mortgage for purchase transactions.  AI Summary

Baby boomers represent 42% of homebuyers and 55% of sellers, according to the most recent data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), yet the mortgage industry has yet to fully account for their presence.

That was the message shared last week by Nora Guerra, senior vice president of community lending solutions at Guild Mortgage, during the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio.

Guerra — who previously worked at Freddie Mac, where she studied how homebuyers change by age group — told the audience that lenders have spent years chasing younger consumers while overlooking older, equity-rich groups who are moving frequently and are in need of help.

“This 55-plus buyer, it’s a main demographic buyer. Everybody has been so focused on the millennial — the older millennial, the younger millennial — and now the Gen Zer,” she said.

Before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, boomers were largely staying put and had few incentives to move, Guerra said. But that changed quickly as single-family home price appreciation skyrocketed from 3.2% in 2019 to 11.3% in 2021 and 11.9% in 2022, according to HousingWire Data.

That contributed heavily to home equity accumulation, with homeowners 62 and older now holding $15.34 trillion in housing wealth, according to NRMLA and RiskSpan. Additionally, the pandemic caused a rupture in many families’ living situations. “They were sheltered in place. They couldn’t see their loved ones, their grandchildren and their children, and it shook them very hard,” Guerra said.

Across years of research, Guerra has uncovered four distinct groups of older homebuyers:

Each of these groups are likely to need financing to accomplish their goals, she said. Reverse mortgages may offer a more cost-effective solution since they don’t require a monthly payment, and they’re often a fit for applicants who’ve been turned down for other types of mortgage credit.

Reverse mortgage for purchase programs, in particular, can fulfill their needs. These products allow seniors to sell their current home and use the equity to buy a similar or more expensive property without monthly payments or the need to pay in cash. “They really don’t know what options are out there, so they feel no one wants to finance me,” Guerra remarked.

According to NAR research cited by Guerra, senior homebuyers frequently utilize mortgages, but the trend wanes as the buyer grows older. The data shows that among 61- to 70-year-olds, 61% financed their purchase during the year ending in June 2025. The percentage dropped to 54% among 71- to 79-year-olds, and to 48% among those 80 and older.

Guerra said mortgage professionals spend too much time discussing problems and not enough time on finding or developing solutions. This can be particularly unhelpful when working with house-rich, cash-poor clients who have significant equity but little in the way of savings or retirement funds.

With these types of needs-based borrowers, reverse mortgage professionals should be asking about the cash they’re looking to access for both everyday living expenses and unexpected expenses. Develop a cash-flow plan based on what they have in their retirement accounts and other investments.

Whether a client is considering a federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage or a proprietary reverse mortgage, counselors certified by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are a key resource to tap into. Guerra said she works with more than 200 counselors nationwide who “help educate and hold the hand of your parent, and tell them all about this program and how it works.”

Originators should ask direct questions about the client’s preferences to pay for their next home, identify any assets they don’t want to touch for that purpose, and offer comparisons of what the financial results will look like with a reverse mortgage versus a cash deal.

Family members often fear there will be nothing left for them when their parent or grandparent dies. But planning ahead of time can help heirs to sell the home and keep any proceeds, or to repay the reverse mortgage and continue living there. Some lenders offer private-label solutions for these exact situations.

Guerra also pointed to NAR data showing that 14% of recent home purchases were tied to multigenerational living situations. These clients often need their family involved when making decisions about reverse mortgages. Adult children want to protect their parents’ assets, so originators should include relatives early in the process.

“Mom and dad haven’t bought a home in the last 10 or 15 years due to lack of inventory. Grandma and grandpa haven’t bought a home in the last 15 to 20 years due to the same reason,” Guerra told the audience. “Multigenerational living is what we’re seeing on these 1003 (loan applications) — lots of grandparents cosigning for their millennial and Gen Z grandchildren if they can afford it, but also lots of gift letters.”

#5416. Sophia Space Deploys Orbital Computing Software Across Multiple Kepler Satellites

First in-space deployment of Sophia Orbital Operating System (SOOS) aboard multiple Kepler Communications satellites opens the door for organizations to run workloads in orbit and accelerate the future of scalable orbital data centers.

PASADENA, Calif., Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sophia Space, a pioneer in passively-cooled orbital computing infrastructure, today announced the first in-space deployment of its Sophia Orbital Operating System (SOOS) leveraging the on-orbit compute infrastructure aboard multiple Kepler satellites within Kepler's Tranche 1 optical data relay constellation. The collaboration is advancing the company's effort to deploy scalable computing infrastructure in orbit. This deployment establishes a foundational software layer for Sophia Space's future orbital computing architecture, designed to support computing workloads across individual spacecraft and larger, distributed orbital networks.

Sophia Space deploys SOOS across multiple Kepler satellites, paving the way for scalable orbital data centers.

Hosted aboard Kepler satellites, the SOOS deployment validates resilient, autonomous software capabilities needed to manage and execute distributed edge computing workloads across multiple spacecraft connected via optical links in the space environment. This software demonstration marks an important step toward dedicated orbital computing infrastructure capable of processing mission-critical data in space, enabling faster insights, greater operational resilience, and more sophisticated space-based data services.

"Building the next generation of space infrastructure isn't about launching an entire data center overnight. It's about proving the architecture, step by step," said Rob DeMillo, CEO and Co-Founder of Sophia Space. "Deploying SOOS in LEO is an important first step. We're beginning with the software foundation, then moving toward dedicated computing hardware, standalone satellites, and ultimately entire constellations. Each mission builds toward a future where computing becomes an integral part of the orbital economy."

The collaboration also highlights the growing convergence of satellite communications and orbital computing, creating opportunities to run AI inference workloads closer to where data is collected and generated. SOOS enables distributed edge computing through managed Kubernetes application deployment and management; software that runs and manages applications across a group of computers. SOOS offers triple redundancy and built-in security capabilities designed to support resilient operations for partners looking to deploy AI inference workloads in orbit across a variety of applications, including missile warning, space domain awareness, maritime awareness, disaster response, atmospheric monitoring and weather intelligence, spacecraft operations, zero-gravity manufacturing, and a host of other potential uses.

"As the space economy grows, communications and computing will become increasingly interconnected," said Caitlin Marsh, president of Kepler US. "Our collaboration with Sophia Space reflects the importance of building an orbital infrastructure ecosystem where data can be processed, managed, and delivered more efficiently. This is an early step toward demonstrating how those capabilities can work together."

SOOS deployment represents the first step in Sophia Space's broader development roadmap, designed to progressively validate the technologies needed to deliver scalable computing infrastructure in orbit. Sophia Space is now open to partner with other companies looking to deploy edge applications in LEO.

"I want to congratulate the software and operations teams at Sophia Space and Kepler for successfully demonstrating distributed operating system functions across multiple satellites in space and multiple GPUs on each satellite," added Dr. Leon Alkalai, Founder and CTO of Sophia Space. "The Sophia team demonstrated distributed functions essential for satellite system resilience, self-awareness and fault tolerance. These building blocks are essential for any future orbiting data centers infrastructure."

These missions are intended to demonstrate how modular computing infrastructure can scale into distributed orbital networks, while advancing opportunities to work with partners to bring new computing capabilities in orbit.

Sophia Space is developing the next generation of orbital computing infrastructure through its modular, passively cooled TILE architecture and Sophia Orbital Operating System (SOOS). Drawing on patented, thermal-management innovations originating at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology, the company is working to make high-performance computing in space more scalable, efficient, and accessible. Headquartered in Pasadena, California, Sophia Space is building the infrastructure to support a growing space-based economy.

Kepler Communications Inc. is a space infrastructure provider on a mission to deliver real-time access to space data. With 33 satellites launched to date, Kepler operates the first commercial optical data relay constellation, enabling real-time, continuous space connectivity while supporting advanced on-orbit compute and hosted payload capabilities. Kepler has achieved industry-leading milestones, including the first commercial on-orbit demonstration of SDA-compatible optical inter-satellite links and successful space-to-air and space-to-ground optical communication demonstrations. Headquartered in Toronto, Canada, Kepler is building a global company to enable the future space economy.

#5415. Reson8 releases Rumble-2-Flash speech model as a free open-weights download

Amsterdam-based speech recognition startup Resonate Labs B.V. today released its Rumble-2-Flash transcription model as a free download with open weights.

Designed for fast transcription of prerecorded audio, the 500 million-parameter model supports more than 40 languages. Reson8 is pitching the release at developers and researchers who need speech recognition built for languages other than English.

According to the company, the leading speech models are trained primarily on English, even though only about one in 20 people speak it as a first language. Specialist terms such as medication names are where accuracy is said to fall furthest once speech moves outside English. Reson8’s models are said to be in production use for meeting notetakers, artificial intelligence receptionists, customer support voice agents, medical transcription and captioning.

“Generic speech models are built for English and make noticeably more mistakes in other languages,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Raoul Ritter, who started the company with Thomas Kluiters and Jarno Verhagen. “Languages like Dutch, Swedish and German are spoken by millions, yet they’re an afterthought.”

Reson8 describes Rumble-2-Flash as one of the smallest models on Hugging Face Inc.’s Open ASR Leaderboard. In the company’s own runs of the leaderboard’s multilingual tests, the model averaged a word error rate of 7.09% across seven languages, including German, French and Dutch. Its average error rate in English is claimed to be about 5%.

On a separate test covering 10 lower-resource languages such as Maltese and Basque, Rumble-2-Flash is said to have posted a mean word error rate of 17.6%. OpenAI Group PBC’s Whisper Large V3 had a mean word error rate of 39.82% on the same test, according to Reson8.

Beyond benchmark sets, Reson8’s models are said to be trained for noisy settings, including phone-line audio. The real world “doesn’t happen in a recording studio,” said Kluiters, the company’s head of AI.

Today’s open-weights release follows the model’s Nov. 3 debut in Reson8’s application programming interface, a week before the company launched its flagship Rumble-2 model. Custom vocabulary support, which lets customers add up to 50,000 terms as text without fine-tuning, remains exclusive to Rumble-2.

Hosted on the company’s own graphics processing units in the Netherlands, Reson8’s service is said to retain no audio or transcripts. The company also claims ISO 27001 certification and compliance with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation and the bloc’s AI Act.

Available free under an Apache 2.0 license, Rumble-2-Flash can also be accessed through Reson8’s API at prices starting from €0.01 ($0.001) per hour of audio.

Reson8 raised €5 million ($5.5 million) in pre-seed funding in March. Balderton Capital led the round, with NP-Hard Ventures also participating. Speech is “quickly becoming a default interface across software,” according to James Wise, a partner at Balderton.

#5414. Why 2027 may turn into a land negotiation year for homebuilders

Scott Cox says 2027 could become a negotiation-driven year in land, with re-trades and real price resets. He argues builders should focus on counterparties’ incentive structures to understand likely outcomes.  AI Summary

In the early ’90s, I worked in Wells Fargo Bank’s real estate workout group in Southern California. The aerospace collapse was crushing the local economy; Los Angeles County alone lost 400,000 jobs. Roughly 25% of WFB’s assets were in commercial real estate (including homebuilding), and another 25% in home mortgages, mostly in California. That was half the bank. Writing off loans and walking away to clean up the books wasn’t an option; we lacked the capital. So we fought for every penny.

We asked for re-margins early on, short-term extensions and collected from borrowers before they ran out of money. We pursued personal guarantees and were willing to fight for them. I realize it is not what an audience of builders wants to hear, but everyone fights to survive.

Bank of America was in a different position. It had less real estate concentration and wanted to expand by buying distressed banks, but it couldn’t until regulators were convinced it had moved past its own problems. So BofA cut deals or foreclosed, cleaning house. Its real estate recovery rate was far lower than ours. That doesn’t mean BofA was wrong. It simply had different incentives.

Everyone knows Charlie Munger’s line, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

We tend to apply it to individuals. But the coming year will be driven largely by company incentives. If you’re a builder, understanding the incentives of the companies across the table may be the most valuable market intelligence you can gather.

Why the coming year? As I’ve said before, I’m not a big fan of short-term market projections. Over longer time spans, demographics, the fundamental balance of supply and demand, and affordability play out; they’re directionally predictable, if not precise. The short term has so many unforeseeable temporary factors that it can, paradoxically, be harder to call. Strategy is for the long term; in the short run, it’s mostly tactics, adapting to what’s in front of you. But caution about predicting short-term conditions is different from dismissing contingency planning.

Housing market conditions have clearly deteriorated. Whatever the cause (war, politics, rising rates or all of the above), I suspect we never had the correction we should have after rates spiked in ’22. A frozen-in-place resale market and the effectiveness of rate buydowns made the following years difficult, but less so than many of us expected.

One of the most intriguing aspects is that I can’t recall a more difficult period in homebuilding (to be clear, I’ve been through far worse, twice) that had so little impact on the land market. The reason was the belief that land was in such short supply that builders couldn’t afford to give up what they had and would need to buy more. Builders weren’t staying in current deals because they necessarily made sense, nor were they buying new ones because they liked the prices.

The attitude was: what’s the alternative?

That belief rested on two assumptions. First, that today’s weakness is a short-term problem: the rate shock would wear off, and buying would pick up. Second, that long-term fundamentals hadn’t changed, so demand would rebound and buoy prices. Either could prove true, but I’m skeptical. As I’ve written over the past year, future demand looks weak relative to the past, not a temporary dip but the start of a regime change. Once that becomes conventional wisdom, why would builders feel the need to control six to seven years of lots? Remember when three to four was considered plenty? Why won’t that be the case again?

I think 2027 is the year land prices will correct, not just terms but real prices. It’s current economics meeting a dawning recognition that the future will need fewer lots. Beyond a few year-end closings, not much will happen in the rest of 2026, and some will wait to see whether a magic spring rebound arrives. But over the last few months, we’ve seen a sharp downgrade in builder expectations for next year. Few expect things to improve soon.

The public builders reinforce this. Many are eliminating forecasts or revising unit counts downward. Much like the difference between making a dollar and losing a dollar, which is much bigger than two dollars, once a builder admits it won’t be growing, it becomes much easier to walk from some positions. Once that threshold is crossed, Wall Street cares far less whether a builder shrinks 2% or 6%.

Reasonable people can differ on this; there are multiple paths forward. But I think the odds are high enough to warrant contingency planning. If I’m right, what happens?

To start, many land bankers (not the old vets, but the newcomers) will learn they weren’t offering a credit product. Like it or not, they’re in real estate and have taken real estate risk. Too many fundamentals in that business were stretched on the belief that big builders wouldn’t walk en masse.

Expect meaningful re-trades, not just extensions. Meanwhile, land sellers will hear builders say they have options and don’t need to rush: “We’ll pay less and take them down on a rolling schedule with a 3% annual escalator. We can’t pay a land banker 10% to hold them; the margin’s too thin.”

That’s where incentives come in. How each negotiation goes will depend heavily on the incentives of the companies involved, and each company has multiple layers. Using land bankers as an example, here are a few questions worth addressing.

How are their asset management fees calculated and collected? As a percentage of revenue, assets (write-downs matter), or cost? Are they amortized over the deal’s life, or literally eat-what-you-kill, paid at closing? Last cycle, it wasn’t uncommon for equity funds to earn asset management fees based on revenue, with half taken up front and the rest amortized over the deal’s projected life.

When deals stretched out, and total revenue fell, the fee shrank and had to last longer. Once it was used up, it was used up, and a manager could be left without enough fee income to run the business but still obligated to manage the assets. That argues for resolving deals. But many of those structures also triggered a true-up at close-out, which argues for delaying resolution. Which pressure drives a given manager? It depends, and that’s exactly why you need to know.

Is their profit from fees or from promotes? A manager who relies on asset management fees will protect them. A manager focused on promotes, with good profits already built up in a tranche, may prefer to resolve an asset quickly, even at a loss, rather than let the overall IRR erode further.

Millrose Properties is an interesting case. Its external manager, Kennedy Lewis (KL), is paid a fee based on the vehicle’s tangible assets rather than on performance, and Millrose is permanent capital with no fund life to force a resolution. That structure rewards keeping the asset base intact; a sale shrinks it, and so does a write-down. I can’t know how KL will respond, and there are counterweights, since Millrose is a public REIT with a dividend and a stock price to consider.

But if I were betting, I’d expect the fee base to weigh heavily. If conditions worsen, few builders will be seeking new land banking, so raising more capital matters less until a recovery brings new deals. One way to keep assets on the books would be to lower option fees and ease takedown terms to keep builders in contract, even at weak returns. A more classic fund structure, by contrast, might push a manager toward resolution rather than managing assets for little or no fee.

Similar dynamics will play out among land sellers. Traditionally, well-capitalized sellers are reluctant to cut prices at first. Doing so immediately crushes expected returns, and the weakness might prove temporary. But at some point, it becomes clear it isn’t temporary, and the concern shifts from return on capital to return of capital.

For fund-backed sellers, the next fundraising effort makes the difference between “we’ve never lost money on a deal” and “we’ve never lost more than 5% on a deal” stark. They don’t read the same in a pitch book. So structures that aren’t ideal from a return perspective get more attention: a lower lot price in exchange for a meaningful true-up or profit participation, with little to no deposit and very soft takedowns. These structures keep open the possibility of at least recovering capital.

How do you learn all this? Ask. Some won’t tell you, but more will than you’d expect. Your counterpart has their own pressures and concerns, and a gentle question can yield a lot of information. Ask before you’re in a workout. If you’re buying, ask what their key motivations are and listen carefully to their answers. In effect, you’re trying to determine whether you’re dealing with a Wells Fargo or a Bank of America.

So, what’s the point of these speculations? Just a reminder that we stand a decent chance of 2027 being the year of negotiations. Understanding the incentive structures of those on the other side of the table may be your most important piece of market intelligence.

#5411. Newrez settles Washington state servicing case with $3 million payout

Newrez reached a consent order with the Washington Department of Financial Institutions resolving allegations of unfair or deceptive mortgage servicing practices from 2021 to 2026. The company will pay just over $3 million, including a $2.5 million payment to DFI, at least $500,000 for consumer remediation and technology upgrades, and an investigation fee.   AI Summary

Newrez agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement broad mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) that the company engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

The consent order, which stems from a multiyear servicing investigation, lands below the $4.175 million civil penalty sought earlier this year by DFI in a statement of charges, but it still represents a significant financial and operational hit for the nonbank servicer.

Newrez does not admit or deny any wrongdoing under the agreement. A company spokesperson told HousingWire the company is “pleased to have resolved this matter.”

“The underlying examination resulted in limited findings, most of which had already been addressed by Newrez. The agreement, which includes no admission of wrongdoing, credits Newrez for several investments made to enhance its operations. We remain committed to supporting homeowners and meeting the high standards they expect,” the spokesperson said.

Under the order, Newrez must pay $2.5 million to DFI, plus at least $500,000 earmarked for consumer remediation and technology and system upgrades. The company also owes an investigation fee of $14,888.90 to cover the agency’s staff time.

The case grew out of more than 125 consumer complaints to DFI, including allegations of unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting at least 29 borrowers. Regulators also cited failures to maintain and service escrow accounts for at least 71 loans to Washington residents.

Earlier charges alleged servicing breakdowns in Washington from 2021 to 2026. These included loan boarding errors that caused private mortgage insurance and escrow problems, misapplied payments, issues with escrow and force‑placed insurance, inaccurate information during foreclosure mediation, faulty statements, and overdue responses to both borrowers and the regulator.

In addition to the monetary obligations, the consent order requires Newrez to undertake affirmative actions across its servicing platform. The company must tighten loan onboarding processes, overhaul core servicing functions, and improve controls over escrow and insurance handling, among other changes. Newrez has to demonstrate to DFI that these corrective actions are complete within 30 days of the order’s effective date.

“Washington state mortgage servicing laws exist to ensure homeowners are treated fairly and that their loans are serviced properly,” DFI Director Charlie Clark said in a statement. “DFI will take action to hold mortgage servicers accountable and will order affirmative action needed to protect Washington homeowners.”

#5410. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5409. The Adecco Group global study: AI delivers more value when people are involved in work redesign

New research among 40,500 workers finds well-integrated AI saves more time, while training, worker involvement and human-centered leadership determine whether adoption translates into sustainable performance.

ZÃRICH, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Adecco Group (SIX: ADEN) today published the seventh edition of its annual Global Workforce of the Future report, based on a survey of 40,500 workers across 36 countries. The findings show that AI adoption is advancing rapidly, but technology delivers its strongest value when organizations redesign work around people; equip them with relevant skills; and give them a voice in how change is implemented.

AI is now embedded in working life. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of workers use AI agents at work, up from 64% in 2025, and technology occupies four of the five leading influences reshaping work. Yet adoption alone does not guarantee value. The research points to a widening gap between organizations that simply deploy AI and those that orchestrate people, AI agents and workflows as a well-orchestrated hybrid workforce.

Where AI is well integrated into operating workflows, workers report saving 20% more time per day than users experiencing lower integration. They are also more likely to reinvest the time saved in higher-value work and seven times less likely to feel overwhelmed by the need to use AI tools effectively. The findings suggest that productivity gains depend less on access to technology than on how effectively it is embedded into the work itself.

Denis Machuel, CEO of the Adecco Group: "The next phase of AI at work is not about deploying more tools. It is about orchestrating people and technology more effectively. When workers help redesign how work gets done, and receive the training and clarity to adapt, AI creates more value and change becomes easier to navigate. AI delivers its greatest impact when it happens with people and not to people."

#5408. Quantum computing drops its decade-away tag as error rates fall 200-fold in two years

Quantum computing is shedding its reputation as speculative as gains in quantum error correction turn fragile machines into reliable ones. For the supercomputing community, which now measures data centers in gigawatts of power, the more pressing question is how quantum fits beside the processors already on the floor.

For years, the field faced a trade-off between speed and reliability, because correcting errors inside a quantum computer slowed it down. That trade-off is fading fast, according to Rajeeb Hazra (pictured), chief executive officer of Quantinuum Inc., which listed on the Nasdaq in June.

“We are now at a stage in 2026 where we have the ability to have tremendous amounts of computation at a very high reliability rate,” Hazra said. “Just two weeks ago, we announced we were doing up to a million operations with five errors. To put it in contrast, just two years ago, we were trying to do 1,000 operations with one error. That’s how fast it is.”

Hazra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed advances in quantum error correction and how AI and quantum computing work in tandem. (* Disclosure below.)

Quantinuum’s 100-qubit Helios system recently set an error-correction record, reaching logical fidelity equivalent to five errors per million operations. The company builds the full stack, from hardware to developer tools, so customers can model problems such as how a drug ages and loses potency, Hazra explained. That positions quantum less as a rival to AI than as a tool AI will lean on for accurate simulation.

“We see AI and quantum working in tandem, or rather AI using quantum computers,” Hazra said. “I don’t think it’s people using quantum computers; it’s AI programming quantum computers to get the data they need to do what AI does best, which is reasoning and prediction.”

Two cloud service providers have already struck deals with Quantinuum, and most of its use-case customers are commercial companies in pharma, energy, chemicals and financial services, Hazra explained. With quantum error correction maturing, the payoff lies in designing materials that release medicine only where the body needs it.

“My view is in five to seven years max, you’re not going to get a prescription for amoxicillin,” Hazra said. “You’re going to get a sheet of paper that basically says this is your pathology. It’ll get matched up at CVS Pharmacy with the available proteins, if you will, and you will get your personalized medicine.”

#5407. Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline

U.S. housing starts rose in October, largely from a 23.6% jump in multifamily starts. Single-family permits fell to 772,000, down 12.9% from a year ago, pointing to slower single-family production ahead.  AI Summary

While October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low.

National housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000.

Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum.

“Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units,” according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington

The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where new home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023.

Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million.

“Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming said in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.”

The new data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400.

Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline.

“Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he said.

The stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023.

Meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025.

Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year.

Year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers.

The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely.

Zillow Senior Economist Kenny Lee noted that the slowdown in single-family starts and permits indicates that homebuilders may be preparing for a relatively weak spring selling season.

“While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane,” Lee explained.

#5406. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5404. AI’s hidden energy tax: More than 80% of scale-up traffic is just memory moving around

Memory bottlenecks are emerging as one of the costliest problems in AI infrastructure as inference overtakes training. GPUs sit idle waiting on data, while high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, stays bolted to processors that cannot share it.

Photonics is shaping up as one way out. Marvell Technology Inc. has been pairing optics with photonic memory to stretch memory beyond the edge of a chip. The payoff is better efficiency in data centers enterprises have already paid for, according to Preet Virk (pictured, left), senior vice president and general manager of the Photonic Fabric Business Unit at Marvell.

“In the data center today, we have a lot of room for improvement of efficiency,” Virk said. “And when I say efficiency, I’m alluding to the wasted flops because we have GPU utilization that’s very low.”

Virk and Andy Mills (right), vice president of advanced product development at Penguin Solutions Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how photonics and shared memory pools can ease memory bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

Penguin’s MemoryAI Photonic Appliance moves HBM into a separate box tens of meters from the GPU, linked by Marvell’s Photonic Fabric. Each appliance holds 16 terabytes of HBM and DDR5 memory that servers across multiple racks can share, Mills explained.

“The challenge there is making sure your LLM doesn’t forget what you started talking to it about 10 minutes ago,” Mills said. “To do that, you need a large amount of memory, large token lengths.”

Optics also changes the energy math. Copper still works inside a rack, but crossing a pod of thousands of GPUs requires optics, according to Virk. More than 80 percent of scale-up network traffic is memory transactions, and a shared pool means much of that data never moves at all, he noted.

“Within data movement, the memory transactions are a place to focus on,” Virk said. “So with this solution versus a copper-based data movement, we could immediately get to a quarter of the energy, picojoules per bit, of data movement.”

Agents raise the stakes, generating far more token requests than human users ever did. As inference spreads across more racks and sites, Mills sees shared pools as the practical answer to memory bottlenecks.

“If anything, distributed encourages shared because you don’t want to recompute,” Mills said. “The whole thing about KV cache was a huge success because it stops recomputation of the same data. And when you can share that data on a broader base and wider across more racks, your efficiencies go up as well.”

#5403. Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows

U.S. building permits fell to a 1,295,000 annual rate in October, with single-family permits at 772,000. With mortgage rates above 7% and builder margins pressured, construction momentum is tracking back toward COVID-era levels.  AI Summary

The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction.

The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021: when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%.

From Census: Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October.As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle.

Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive.

One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product.

New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years.

Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more.

#5401. Dubai International Chamber opens representative office in Miami to strengthen trade and investment ties between Dubai and the United States

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dubai International Chamber, one of the three chambers operating under the umbrella of Dubai Chambers, has opened a new representative office in Miami. The office aims to strengthen business ties between Dubai and the United States and expand trade and investment cooperation between companies in both markets.

The Miami office is Dubai International Chamber's second representative office in the United States, following the opening of its New York office during the Dubai Business Forum â USA, organised by Dubai Chambers in November 2025.

Salem AlShamsi, Executive Vice President of International Relations at Dubai Chambers, stated: "The opening of our new office in Miami marks an important step towards expanding trade and investment partnerships between Dubai and the United States and creating new growth opportunities for the business communities in both markets".

The new office comes amid growing trade between Dubai and the United States. Bilateral non-oil trade reached AED 121.8 billion in 2025, representing an increase of 4.6% compared to the previous year.

The number of active American companies registered with Dubai Chamber of Commerce reached 3,718 by the end of December 2025, recording year-on-year growth of 18.1%. A further 439 American companies joined the chamber during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting continued interest among American businesses in Dubai as a destination for business, expansion, and investment.

The Miami office will strengthen engagement with key public and private sector stakeholders, deepen cooperation with the American business community, and highlight the competitive advantages that make Dubai a leading global business destination. It will also provide information and market intelligence to help American companies enter the Dubai market and expand their operations from the city into international markets.

In addition, the office will support Dubai-based companies seeking to expand into the United States by providing specialised market insights, helping them identify promising trade and investment opportunities, and connecting them with trusted local partners.

Dubai International Chamber, one of the three chambers operating under the umbrella of Dubai Chambers, was established to promote Dubai as a global business hub, attract multinational companies and expand the emirate's trade ties with promising markets.

#5400. Unsiloed nabs $7.5M to turn scanned documents into structured data for AI agents

Document-scanning firm Unsiloed Inc. today announced it has raised $7.5 million in seed funding to turn PDFs and other complex documents into structured, readable data for artificial intelligence agents.

Participants in the round, led by Felicis, included Y Combinator, Orange Collective, Uncorrelated Ventures, Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner.

A variety of documents arrive in formats that are not straight data or text. Financial statements, insurance claims, contracts, clinical records, and operational forms make up the constellation of critical information for everyday business and operations. This information could be stored as images, PDFs or other formats and include charts, layouts and other elements that don’t translate directly into text.

Determining which column or axis of a chart belongs to which row, which heading leads which clause, or whether a pull quote interrupts the flow of the text or appears at the end of the document becomes a question of how to store the information.

Unsiloed parses documents such as PDFs using intelligent visual-first scanning to understand structured tables, sections and parent-child relationships between text. The company, which describes itself as intelligence-directed and vision-first, technology can scan forms, presentations, Word files and images into Markdown or JSON, a JavaScript Object Notation standard format readily readable by large language models.

“We believe AI agents will eventually read and write more documents than humans,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Aman Mishra. “Those agents do not just need better OCR. They need a dynamic interface to read, update and act on unstructured data.”

OCR, or optical character recognition, is the standard technology that is used to convert physical or image-based text, such as scanned paper documents or PDFs, into digital text. However, OCR doesn’t recognize tables, graphics or layouts; it only pre-processes the document to identify text, recognizes text and then outputs a contextual stream based on what it sees.

Unsiloed goes a step further by accounting for the page’s layout and format and providing a structured, machine-readable document that inherits the document’s original features. This means that if the presentation included headings, charts or other parts that relate to one another, those relationships are included in the data.

OCR is the most common way companies digitize documents today; Unsiloed believes it can do it better.

The company’s parser rated an 88.0 score on the olmOCR-Bench benchmark, a benchmark published by the Allen Institute for AI that is a rigorous, reproducible evaluation of how well modern AI models handle real-world OCR challenges. Compared with other services, Unsiloed said, it stacks up extremely well; for example, Anthropic PBC’s Claude Opus 4.7 ranks at 81.9, OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT 5.5 ranks at 84.6 and Google LLC’s Gemini 3 Pro ranks at 77.7.

“We combine deterministic computer vision algorithms with dual-stream vision models to build the interface that ranked first among 19 systems on olmOCR-Bench for AI agents to interact with unstructured data,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Adnan Abbas.

The company said its dual-stream vision architecture allows it to process content and visual layouts at the same time. Developers can upload custom schemas to extract fields, classify and split documents, and update text and images while preserving document formatting.

It said it has processed millions of pages of documents for organizations across industries, from early-stage AI startups to banks, publicly traded insurance companies and law firms. The platform supports private-cloud, on-premises and fully air-gapped machines, allowing enterprise organizations to build Unsiloed into their document pipeline and do processing on their own infrastructure.

“We’ve significantly enhanced accuracy, context understanding, and response quality across all knowledge-base-powered conversations,” said Prateek Sachan, founder and CTO of Bolna AI, a company that builds voice agents for languages spoken across India.

#5399. Fix-and-flip margins tighten in Q3 as prices dip and costs rise

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index dropped to 53 in Q3 2026, the lowest reading in nearly 4 years. Investors cited mortgage rates above 7%, softer prices and labor constraints that pressured margins.  AI Summary

The U.S. fix-and-flip market weakened in the third quarter as mortgage rates above 7% slowed buyer demand, while falling home prices and higher labor costs squeezed investors’ margins, according to a survey from Kiavi and John Burns Research and Consulting.

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index fell to a reading of 53 in the third quarter, down from 59 in the second quarter and 56 a year earlier. The index, which measures market conditions on a scale of 0 to 100, reached its lowest level in nearly four years.

Readings below 50 indicate market contraction, while readings above 50 indicate expansion. The November 2026 report is based on a proprietary quarterly survey of approximately 280 fix-and-flip investors.

Only 23% of flippers expect good sales over the next six months, the lowest share in four years. Meanwhile, 19% anticipate poor sales, the highest share since Q4 2022.

The slowdown is affecting investors of different sizes. Large flippers, defined as those who bought or sold at least eight homes over the previous 18 months, reported worse market conditions than smaller operators for the first time since Q3 2022.

Higher mortgage rates have also reduced pricing power for investors. Forty percent of flippers said home sale prices in their markets were lower than a year earlier, compared with 16% who reported higher prices. Another 36% said prices were largely unchanged.

The Southwest reported the greatest share of flippers experiencing lower prices, at 67%, followed by Southern California at 50%. In Texas and the Southeast, 47% reported lower prices, while 44% of Florida respondents said the same.

About one in five flippers said they were selling homes mostly below their initial after-repair value estimates, approaching the highest level recorded by the survey since 2021.

The survey also found that immigration enforcement is affecting renovation labor availability and costs. Forty-one percent of flippers said increased immigration enforcement had negatively affected their labor force, up from 33% when the question was asked in Q2 2025.

Respondents reported difficulties finding workers, higher labor costs and longer project timelines. The impact was particularly pronounced in Florida and the Southeast, although flippers in other regions also reported challenges.

More available inventory is creating additional acquisition opportunities for investors. Twenty-four percent of flippers said competition for deals was lower than usual, the highest share in the survey’s history.

Despite the increased availability, investors remain cautious about how much they’re willing to pay. The average flipper targeted a maximum purchase price of 67% of a property’s after-repair value, down slightly from the previous quarter.

Renovation costs also varied significantly by region. The national average cost per flipped home was $72,000 in the third quarter, with costs reaching $133,000 in Southern California and $86,000 in the Northeast. Costs were lower in the Southeast and Texas, at $47,000 and $46,000, respectively.

The survey’s findings point to continued pressure on investors as higher financing costs, weaker buyer demand and labor constraints complicate project economics. As a result, John Burns recommended that flippers remain disciplined when acquiring properties and build in sufficient margins to account for potential price declines and higher labor expenses.

The firm also advised lenders to underwrite properties based on expected sale prices at the time of disposition rather than relying solely on recently closed comparable sales, which can lag in a declining market.

#5398. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

#5396. Agents want the crown jewels: HPE and Daxa push governance down to the data layer

Enterprises are handing AI agents their most sensitive data, and governance is struggling to keep pace. Techniques such as semantic caching are emerging as a way to enforce controls inline without slowing agents down.

Moving agents from pilot to production means letting them read, change and even delete the records that matter most. That shift makes data access the central security question for agentic AI, according to Huseni Saboowala (pictured, right), co-founder and chief executive officer at Daxa Inc.

“For agents to really get to value, they need to be able to interact with your real enterprise data, and that includes your crown jewels, your intellectual property, your customer data in your [customer relationship management] and your proprietary trading algorithms,” he said. “That creates an unprecedented level of risk for enterprises because the agents are not just reading data; they’re also able to now go manipulate data at scale.”

Saboowala and Robin Braun (left), vice president of AI business development at Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., spoke with theCUBE’s Enterprise Editor, Paul Gillin, during coverage of SC26 on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Daxa is a partner in HPE’s Unleash AI program, which offers pre-validated software on HPE Private Cloud AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Firewalls, data loss prevention and identity management still have a job to do. But they were built for users and applications, not software that reasons over data, Saboowala explained.

“Those agents are operating, though, at layer 8, what we call the cognitive layer,” he said. “This is where you have the prompts, the responses, the retrievals and the tool calls happening. Traditional tools really are not operating at this layer.”

Saboowala’s answer is reasoning-based access controls, backed by agents that flag abnormal behavior. HPE builds governance into its Private Cloud AI stack from the start, according to Braun.

“Being able to build in that governance from day one allows you to understand what is it going to look like so that … you’re not bolting it on later,” she said. “Instead, it’s a part of the workflow.”

Timing matters as much as policy. Offline governance arrives too late for agents working at machine speed, so enforcement must happen inline through semantic caching, specialized small language models and a distributed data plane, Saboowala explained. A regional bank that deployed Daxa with HPE has since connected its agents to source code and regulated customer data.

“I believe that the winners in this agent era are not just the ones who have the most [graphics processing units],” Saboowala said. “But they will be enterprises who have agents they can trust with their data.”
