#5395. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5391. AI factories push liquid cooling beyond CPUs and GPUs to nearly every rack component

The liquid cooling supply chain is under mounting pressure as AI factories pack more heat into every rack.

To meet demand, operators have invested heavily in denser racks and liquid cooling, as well as the hoses and couplings that move the fluid must arrive faster and in larger volumes than ever. But for component makers, keeping up takes more than extra shifts. With liquid cooling reaching more of the rack, equipment makers need connections suited to a wider range of components, according to Tyler Glenn (pictured, right), engineer, product applications and data centers, at Danfoss Power Solutions, a division of Danfoss A/S.

“We went from air cooling to hybrid cooling and we’re moving a lot now towards full liquid cooling,” Glenn said. “Traditionally, it was just the CPUs and GPUs that were being liquid cooled. But as more components are starting to have to get integrated, there’s a lot more opportunity for us to have different types of connections to solve specific challenges that this industry faces.”

Glenn and Lauren Witter (left), vice president of sales at Omni Services Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the liquid cooling supply chain, the universal quick disconnect and designing systems for rising heat density. (* Disclosure below.)

When a rush order comes in for a large data center build, suppliers need parts on hand to assemble hoses quickly, Glenn explained. Danfoss works with distributors that carry its hoses and couplings to keep a minimum stock available as part of a strategy to stay ahead of projections

“A lot of times our customers will provide us forecasts, but we like to shoot above that and look ahead and make sure that in case that the demand increases beyond that, that we’re prepared for that,” Glenn said. “When it comes to our component suppliers, we’re making sure to order additional materials, but also keeping track of making sure we have enough stock.”

But when a data center builder needs parts for denser AI racks on short notice, having stock on hand gives distributors a head start. Omni’s CoolFlow division works directly with Danfoss’s data center team to handle those requests, according to Witter. Both teams focus on liquid cooling, so Omni can take a rush order straight to the engineers it already works with.

“No one gets frustrated when we’re calling Tyler saying we need these parts yesterday,” Witter said. “They get it. They’re playing the same game we are.”

#5389. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5387. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5386. AI’s GPU focus meets a CPU reality check at Dell and AMD

Agentic AI is rewriting the business development playbook for chipmakers and server builders. Graphics processing units still grab the headlines, but as supercomputing and AI converge, the next wave of demand is landing on central processing units that must fit within data centers’ existing power budgets.

The shift has been building for years. Customers that hung more GPUs off a single CPU found they were starving expensive accelerators of data, leaving them idle, according to Scott Tease (pictured, left), vice president of business development for high-performance computing and sovereign AI at Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

“People have realized how important that CPU is in a GPU architecture. But beyond that, agentic is not necessarily just a GPU thing,” Tease said. “Agentic is going to be very CPU heavy because with agentic, what you’re looking at, you want to go very fast, but you also want concurrency.”

Tease and David Schmidt (right), vice president of PowerEdge product management at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the growing role of CPUs in agentic workloads and the challenges of balancing compute performance with data center power constraints. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell and AMD have been building rack-scale AI platforms together, but power remains the binding constraint. When Dell began planning its portfolio 2.5 years ago, enterprise customers expected rack power requirements to remain at 15 to 20 kilowatts and said they often ran out of power before filling a rack, according to Schmidt. Dell responded with the PowerEdge R9825, a 3U server built on AMD’s sixth-generation EPYC 9006 processors.

“It’s been optimized for power efficiency and cooling efficiency,” Schmidt said. “That means we’re using less power to cool the system overall, and that’s power that we can return to our customers.”

That efficiency compounds at refresh time. A single EPYC 9006 server can take 13 legacy machines out of production while cutting the system power needed for cooling by 80 percent, Schmidt noted. Tease sees reclaimed power feeding agentic workloads, where agents could turn one researcher’s ideas into thousands of compute jobs.

“Same number of researchers, massive increase in the amount of compute. Agentic is going to continue to drive more and more IT, and we’ve got to find a way to power it,” Tease said.

BENGALURU, India and KOLKATA, India and NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Happiest Minds Technologies Limited ("Happiest Minds") (NSE: HAPPSTMNDS), an AI First, customer-centric digital engineering company, today announced the deployment of its cloud-native digital banking platform, Arttha, to support selected capabilities within Spark by Absa, the digital banking and lifestyle app from Absa Bank (Mauritius) Limited.

Developed and built in Mauritius, Spark is proudly 'Made in Moris' and brings payments, banking services, offers and lifestyle experiences together for Absa and non-Absa customers.

Arttha's Open Banking and Financial Marketplace modules power selected Spark capabilities, including account linking, payment options, offers and experience bookings. Happiest Minds provided technical integration and implementation support, while Absa Mauritius led the development of the Spark proposition and customer experience.

Arttha is Happiest Minds Technologies' cloud-native digital banking platform, supporting banks and financial technology companies across markets with capabilities spanning payments, lending, core banking and open banking.

Joseph Anantharaju, Co-Chairman & CEO, Happiest Minds Technologies, said: "The launch of Spark by Absa reflects the strength of our relationship with Absa Mauritius and our shared commitment to making digital services more relevant and accessible. Through Arttha, we are pleased to provide the underlying platform capabilities that support the bank in bringing its vision for Spark by Absa to market and creating greater value for customers in their everyday lives."

Prathamesh Kulkarni, CEO, BFSI, Healthcare & Life Sciences, and Retail & CPG, Happiest Minds Technologies, added: "Arttha is an important part of our digital banking portfolio. Its deployment in support of Spark by Absa demonstrates how underlying technology platforms can support banks in responding to changing customer needs and delivering more connected digital experiences. We value the opportunity to support Absa Mauritius as it advances its digital strategy."

Udeet Bhagat, Arttha Business Head, Happiest Minds Technologies, said: "Absa has been a valued customer in Arttha's growth journey, and the launch of Spark by Absa further strengthens this relationship. Arttha provides selected underlying platform capabilities that support Absa Mauritius' proposition, bringing banking, payments and lifestyle services closer together with the customer at the centre."

Yousuf Hoossainsaeb, Head of Open Banking at Absa Bank (Mauritius) Limited, said: "Spark by Absa reflects our ambition to play a more meaningful role in our customers' everyday lives. Conceived, designed and built in Mauritius, Spark is proudly Made in Moris and shaped around the evolving needs of our market. It brings payments, banking services, offers and lifestyle experiences together within one convenient digital platform.

Happiest Minds supports Spark through selected underlying technology capabilities and technical integration expertise. At its heart, Spark is about using technology to address real needs and create value beyond traditional banking."

For Happiest Minds, the deployment of Arttha in support of Spark by Absa marks a further step in its relationship with Absa. It also demonstrates the role that underlying technology platforms can play in supporting banks as they introduce digital propositions that respond to changing customer expectations.

The collaboration combines Absa Mauritius' locally conceived and built Spark proposition and customer experience with selected underlying platform capabilities from Arttha and technical integration support from Happiest Minds. Spark remains a distinctly Mauritian proposition, created in Mauritius for the evolving needs of the local market.

#5384. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5383. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event

AI workflow automation is changing how businesses build applications and manage everyday work, raising questions about the role of established software platforms. As organizations experiment with AI-generated applications and autonomous agents, they must also determine how to maintain access controls, integrate existing systems and manage increasingly complex workflows.

The growing accessibility of AI development tools has prompted speculation that businesses could replace traditional software-as-a-service platforms with applications built for specific needs. But building an application and operating it securely across an enterprise present different challenges, according to Casey George, chief revenue officer of monday.com Ltd.

“We are seeing customers come back to a platform that’s integrated — that’s governed, that’s permissioned with their infrastructure, that is secure — like monday.com,” he told theCUBE. “I joke and say it was an expensive funeral, but we learned a lot. Customers learned a lot.”

George, along with executives and practitioners, spoke with host Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined enterprise AI deployment, governance requirements and the challenges of scaling AI workflow automation across organizations. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Casey George:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event:

Making autonomous agents available to employees does not guarantee business returns. After an internal initiative produced more than 3,600 agents, monday.com established monday Frontier, an organization combining managed services and deployment engineers to help customers identify workflow bottlenecks and implement AI projects. The initiative addresses the implementation challenges involved in moving agents into productive use, according to Eran Zinman (pictured), co-founder and co-chief executive officer of monday.com.

“Adopting AI really requires expertise. I know how hard it is because we experienced ourselves that you have this amazing technology, but how do you actually use it?” he said during the event.

As organizations deploy AI agents, security teams must account for how access rights change across users, applications and environments. Incremental rollouts offer a way to test capabilities before expanding their reach, while permission management remains an ongoing responsibility, according to Ryan Nigro, security trust and enablement team lead at monday.com.

“It just comes to making sure that your users are properly being given just enough to do their roles but not too much to cause harm,” Nigro told theCUBE. “There’s no reason why a sales rep should have the ability to change your production environment.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Ryan Nigro:

At Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., employees are using monday vibe, monday.com’s no-code application builder, to create custom tools. One executive dashboard replaces the manual process of copying charts into presentation slides while retaining the ability to export to PowerPoint, according to Kate Kenner, capability and community lead for strategic sourcing and planning at HPE.

“[Executives] knocked a whole bunch of the meetings off the calendar,” she told theCUBE. “Instead of weekly, now they’re monthly.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Kate Kenner:

At Lowe’s Cos. Inc., coordinating store setups and remodels once required tracking information across Microsoft Excel, emails and other communications. The retailer now uses monday.com to monitor individual store bays and dozens of simultaneous projects, according to Lanny Finley, director of remerch and new stores at Lowe’s.

“I can take the dashboard and see which projects are on track, which ones are at risk, and then make the appropriate actions and get the right partners in place to make the corrections to get everything back on track and completed,” he said during the event.

Lowe’s also developed an internal Green Dot Board to track issues such as missing components during store projects. The company is exploring additional automation that could initiate vendor orders when components are needed and close issues once replacements are installed, according to Brian Olms, senior business partner manager at Lowe’s, who joined Finley during the discussion.

“We needed a way to automate the process, make it more user-friendly [and] make it simpler. That’s what we started the Green Dot Board for,” he told theCUBE. “Here at Elevate, we’re seeing ways that we could even take it a step further and start to use agents and more automation and [the] vibe app.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Lanny Finley and Brian Olms:

For nonprofits facing growing demand, AI workflow automation offers a way to expand organizational capacity without placing additional administrative burdens on employees. At Feed the Children Inc., a two-person team oversees relationships with more than 500 community partners, according to Colleen Finn Ridenhour, chief growth and strategy officer at Feed the Children.

“Things from [memorandums of understanding] and legal contracts, annual renewals and compliance and reporting — it’s quite a lot. It’s been a very manual process, historically, for them to keep track of that all the time. We really want them focused on the human element of that job, which is bringing in new partners to help us scale our impact,” she told theCUBE.

The nonprofit uses monday.com’s forms, boards, automations and agents to coordinate partner activities and manage information. Employees can also build dashboards for specific needs, including budget tracking, while retaining human oversight of compliance-related work, according to Ridenhour.

“We’re not going to be able to scale our impact by just always asking people to work harder. [We need to find] ways to repeat a lot of these repetitive actions in a much easier way and [share] information so [that] people’s jobs get easier and it frees up their time to do the things that only they can do,” she said during the event.

#5380. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

#5379. Recent spate of outages attributed to technical issues amid accelerated AI bug discovery

U.S. authorities don’t believe that the recent outages at federal agencies and top tech firms were caused by cyberattacks.

The Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, Apple Inc. and Microsoft Corp. were among the affected organizations. All four said that their systems were disrupted by technical issues rather than hackers. Experts noted that artificial intelligence models’ ability to find software bugs has made patching more complicated, which may increase the risk of outages.

The first major service disruption hit Exchange Online on Thursday. The Microsoft-operated email service went offline for nearly a day, which left 450 million users without access to their inboxes. The company attributed the downtime to two separate bugs in the software that powers its network. The first one went undetected for three months, while the other cropped up a day before the outage.

The FAA experienced a network disruption of its own on Friday. An issue with a router at the agency’s El Dorado, Arkansas campus disrupted aircraft communications and radar data feeds. The outage led to more than 12,000 flight cancellations.

United Airlines reported a fairly extensive, but brief infrastructure disruption a few days later. The issue took several of the carrier’s pilot-facing applications offline for 30 minutes. Fewer than 150 flights were affected.

Yet another high-profile network outage occurred on Tuesday, this time at the U.S. National Security Agency. A technical problem cropped up in NSANet, an internal network that agency staff use to exchange classified information. The cause of the outage and its duration were not specified. However, officials did tell NBC the disruption wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.

U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that point in a Tuesday interview. He added that officials have “looked very closely” into the other outages that occurred over the past week and ruled out cyberattacks as the cause. According to Clayton, authorities believe that the disruptions occurred because companies are patching vulnerabilities “on much larger scale” than before.

Frontier AI models have found thousands of software vulnerabilities over the past few months. That accelerated pace of discovery is creating more work for administrators, who have to roll out patches more frequently than before. The less time there is to prepare a patch, the greater the risk of human error.

“As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and development cycles, pressure is mounting on companies to deploy fixes quickly, often without fully understanding how those changes will affect interconnected systems, “ said Prince Kohli, the chief executive officer of software testing provider Sauce Labs Inc. “The only way to prevent these issues is continuous testing and release validation in their development processes, even more so for critical software updates.”

Apple and Workday Inc. are also among the companies that have experienced outages in recent days. Separately, several financial services temporarily became unavailable because of an issue with one of JPMorgan Chase’s on-premises systems. All the incidents have been resolved.

#5377. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5376. AI Search Is Tipping The Balance In Favor Of Big-Box Stores. Here’s How Small Retailers Can Fight Back

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI search overwhelmingly favors major retailers. Small merchants can take these three steps to get noticed by chatbots.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

A new study we commissioned shows that nine times out of 10, AI directs shoppers to major retailers. Looking to buy a new road bike in New York? Chances are, ChatGPT will provide a list of national chains, even when there’s a great independent store just around the corner. The buyer didn’t ask for that kind of list. The model decided for them.

For the past two decades, being discoverable online revolved around SEO. The basic question was: Are you showing up in Google results? Search engines learned shoppers’ locations and surfaced nearby businesses.

Those priorities shouldn’t disappear just because answers now come from chatbots. If AI platforms are becoming the new front door to commerce, they share responsibility for which businesses get found.

But small retailers can’t afford to wait for these companies to refine their search results. AI is changing the rules, and stores need to keep up. They have to think not only about whether search engines can find them, but whether AI understands who they are, what they sell, and why they’re worth recommending.

One place to start is by educating customers. Our study found that adding words like “independent” or “locally owned” to AI searches reduced big chains’ share of recommendations to as little as one in 10 on Google’s platforms.

Retailers can spread the word by sharing simple search tips with shoppers in-store, on their websites, and across social media. The more consumers make independent businesses a priority in their searches, the stronger the signal to AI companies that local options deserve greater visibility.

Beyond educating shoppers, here are three more things merchants can do to raise their profile in AI search.

To get AI’s attention, small retailers also need to give them something to find. And the closer a shopper gets to making a purchase, the tougher the competition becomes. Our study showed that when someone names a specific product, a small store’s odds of being the top recommendation fall from roughly one in three to one in 10.

Big retailers also have an advantage when it comes to how much information about them is readily available online. Their catalogs, inventory, product descriptions, reviews, and locations are already highly visible. Small merchants may have deeper expertise and better curation, but AI can’t recommend what it can’t see.

That makes it even more important for retailers to put their inventory online. AI agents increasingly fetch product information directly, which means retail websites may effectively become showrooms for both AI and human shoppers.Here, AI is part of the solution. New tools let retailers showcase their entire product catalog so agents can find what they’re looking for. Besides syncing that inventory with your POS, they write descriptions that make those products easier for AI to discover.

Making a retail website simple for AI to read is critical, too. Behind the scenes, a merchant can clearly label product details like price, brand, and whether an item is in stock, while also giving search and AI crawlers a map of the pages it wants them to find.

When shoppers use an AI chatbot to search, they ask a lot of questions. What jacket styles are hot this fall? Which supportive running shoes are best for beginners? What are the top ergonomic office chairs for working from home?

For independent retailers, that creates another opportunity to get noticed. The key is to establish yourself as an expert by building authority around what you sell.

Useful, substantive content can help. For example, a bike shop could create TikTok or YouTube videos showing how to set up tubeless tires or replace a worn chain. Those clips may look educational, but what they’re really doing is showing the expertise behind the business.

Of all the social platforms, YouTube could be an independent merchant’s best friend. Just ask the small luxury watch dealers who use long-form informational videos to build trust — by exploring topics like how to avoid buying a fake.

YouTube’s connection to Google makes it an even more powerful tool for independent retailers. Gemini regularly surfaces videos from the site, giving merchants another way to get their expertise (and products) in front of shoppers using AI search.

A steady stream of blog posts can do the same thing. By posting weekly about fashion trends, for instance, a women’s clothing boutique gives AI systems more proof that it knows its category inside and out.

If that sounds like a heavy lift, it doesn’t need to be. AI assistants can help write, publish, and manage blog content, while built-in SEO tools help optimize each post for traditional search and make it easier for search engines to crawl and AI systems to understand.

To stand out in AI search, small retailers also need to rethink what social media is for.

Platforms like Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube still help stores reach shoppers. But they now do a second job: showing AI what a business sells, what it knows, and what it specializes in.

AI tools are paying attention. Social posts appear in almost 70% of Google’s AI Overview responses. And in Google’s AI mode, they show up in almost half of responses to searches that don’t name a brand — the ones shoppers type before they know your store exists.Meta’s new Muse agent takes this further. Muse works inside Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, which reach 3.6 billion people a day. With a shopper’s permission, it can learn their taste from what they follow, like, save, and share. Every customer who engages with a store’s posts is teaching their agent that the store belongs on their shortlist. Retailers with active, engaged communities are more likely to be recommended.

That’s the real opening for local retailers: AI remembers what shoppers like. Once a customer shows their agent they value a certain kind of store, like a neighborhood bookshop or an independent boutique, it can keep recommending similar places.

For their part, retailers should show up consistently where both shoppers and AI are paying attention. By embracing this new reality, they can turn a potential threat into a reason for customers to make the trip.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

#5375. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5373. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:38 am

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

#5372. This 54-Year-Old Left Her Full-Time Therapist Job to Focus on a Flavorful Side Hustle Making $10K a Month on Amazon: ‘I Used ChatGPT’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lana Wimmer wanted to bring a different kind of beverage to market.

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lana Wimmer, 54, of St. George, Utah. She started her side hustle Öl Brew (pronounced “cool” without the “c”), a nonalcoholic sparkling fruit malt beverage, while working about 40 hours a week as a mental health therapist. Once she caught herself sitting in a therapy session thinking about Öl Brew, she knew she had to focus on the business full-time. The brand generates about $10,000 a month in revenue on Amazon.  Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

When did you launch the side hustle, and what specific consumer pain point did you want to address? We launched Öl Brew in 2026, about six months ago, but the idea had been with me for eight years. For most of that time, I kept hoping someone else would make these drinks. I had absolutely no ambition to enter the beverage industry.

My husband and I had lived in Europe and the Middle East, where we’d discovered nonalcoholic fruit malt beverages with this wonderful depth, body and flavor. They were nothing like the sodas we had back home. When we returned to the U.S., I couldn’t find anything that compared. The options felt uninspired: soda, sparkling water or a mocktail trying awfully hard to replace alcohol. I didn’t want an imitation of something else. I wanted a genuinely different drinking experience.

How did you validate that people would actually pay for your solution before investing serious money?One evening, I finally shared my idea over dinner with friends. The response was immediate. Everyone wanted better nonalcoholic options; this wasn’t just my personal preference.

I was also watching a shift in consumer behavior, particularly among my own adult children and their friends. They weren’t gathering around alcohol. They were cold plunging, working out and training for HYROX competitions. Their social lives looked different, and so did their beverage choices. Having spent decades as a therapist, I was especially interested in what was driving that shift. People were becoming more intentional about how they spent their time, what they consumed and how they connected.

Those early conversations gave me the conviction to invest although they weren’t proof of purchase. That came later when we got the product onto shelves and watched customers respond. Sometimes you recognize a gap in the market because you’ve been standing in it for years.

Which two or three essential tools, apps or pieces of gear did you buy in your first week, and which ones did you skip to save money?My first tools were a notebook, my computer and ChatGPT. I started writing down everything I wanted to build, followed by a much longer list of everything I didn’t know.

I used ChatGPT to research flavor houses, co-packers, brand management companies, distributors and how the beverage industry actually works. It helped me learn the terminology, understand the process and figure out whom I needed to talk to. But the real education came when I started taking those questions to people with experience. AI gave me a starting point. Industry professionals gave me context, perspective and occasionally some very expensive lessons.

I also listened constantly to business and beverage podcasts, particularly The Game with Alex Hormozi, Tim Bush’s On the Shelf and Joey Pedone’s Sippin’ & Selling. I didn’t spend money on elaborate software systems or expensive subscriptions in the beginning. My priority was understanding the business well enough to make informed decisions. I learned quickly that information is relatively easy to find. Knowing what to do with it is another matter entirely.

What were the first three steps you took in your first 30 days?My first 30 days were focused on three things: Developing a go-to-market plan, identifying our target consumer and first four flavors, and finding the people who could help bring the product to life.

I used AI to help research the industry and build an initial strategy. Then I settled on apple, lemon, peach and pomegranate as our first flavors. I wanted something familiar enough that people would be curious to try it, but different enough that they’d immediately recognize this wasn’t ordinary soda.

Then came the investment. I spent $50,000 hiring a beverage development company to help formulate the drinks and connect us with a co-packer. I also hired a branding company to develop our can designs and brand book. Altogether, the initial upfront cost, including the pilot run and production run, was about $200,000.

Here’s what I learned later: The formulation work could have been arranged without that fee. I didn’t know that at the time. That was an expensive introduction to an industry where relationships, experience and knowing the right questions to ask can save you a tremendous amount of money.

How did you land your first paying customer?Our first paying customer came after our pilot run and initial production, and there was nothing sophisticated about the sales strategy. We walked into a local grocery store, sat down with the manager, introduced ourselves and told him what we were building. He agreed to carry Öl Brew.

Another local farmers market retailer followed, and suddenly our drinks were on shelves, where actual customers could decide if our idea had merit. Those first accounts gave us more than revenue. They gave us feedback, credibility and the opportunity to start building a business in the real world.

After all the planning, design, and money we’d spent, our first sale came from sitting across a table and having a conversation. I rather love that.

Nowadays, which specific tools or platforms help you bring in customers, and what is one feature inside those tools that saves you the most time?We’re using Instagram, TikTok Shop, Amazon, Walmart.com and our Shopify website to introduce consumers to Öl Brew and drive sales. Because we’re bringing an entirely new beverage experience to the American market, our marketing has to do more than create awareness. We have to give people a reason to be curious. Most consumers understand soda. They understand sparkling water. But sparkling fruit malt soda? That’s a conversation starter.

On the operational side, Klaviyo has been particularly useful for automating customer communication through Shopify. We can capture email addresses, create welcome sequences, share promotions and maintain relationships without manually managing every interaction. That kind of automation matters when you’re running lean.

What was the single biggest bottleneck that almost stalled your business, and what exact change or process fixed it?Distribution has been our biggest challenge. The beverage industry has a complicated relationship between retailers and distributors. Retailers want to know who’s distributing your product. Distributors increasingly want retail authorizations before they’ll take on a new brand. Which leaves emerging brands trying to convince both sides to move first.

We would attend trade shows and return with interest from eight distributors across the country. The conversations were promising, the enthusiasm was real, and then everything would stall because we didn’t yet have the retail commitments to support distribution. It was frustrating and forced us to reconsider our approach.

We realized we needed to focus less on how many distributors were interested and more on securing actual retail placements. That meant targeting independent stores and smaller retailers more willing to take a chance on something new. We also brought on an experienced VP of sales to help sharpen our strategy, prioritize accounts and build a more disciplined approach to retail expansion. It’s a significant shift, and we’re beginning to see a clearer path forward.

How many months did it take to reach consistent monthly revenue, and what was your average monthly profit during your first six months?We’re still working toward consistent monthly revenue. We’re only a few months into launch, and building a beverage brand requires significant capital long before the revenue catches up. But we’ve had encouraging early traction.

During Sober October, Öl Brew reached No. 14 in a nonalcoholic beverage ranking on Amazon. We also generated approximately $10,000 in Amazon revenue during October, just months after launching on the platform.

We’re not yet consistently profitable. We’re investing in inventory, marketing, distribution and the team we need to support growth. There’s a part of entrepreneurship that rarely makes it into the success stories: the period when you’re spending money, making adjustments and trying to determine which investments will actually produce results. That’s where we are.

What is your current monthly revenue and profit margin? We’re about six months into launch, with Amazon generating approximately $10,000 in monthly revenue, plus additional sales through retail and other ecommerce channels. We’re still investing heavily in growth, so we haven’t established a consistent net profit margin.

What part of the work do you still handle yourself, and which tasks have you outsourced?As for my time, I spend roughly 10 hours a day on Öl Brew, often more. My work falls into three main areas: brand awareness, retail and distribution, and manufacturing and operations. We’ve outsourced Amazon optimization and SEO, TikTok Shop management and creator partnerships, and much of our branding, marketing and social media execution.

If someone is starting from scratch today, what are common beginner mistakes they should avoid?Don’t rush into hiring. I made the mistake of trusting people who promised far more than they could deliver. Some were convincing, experienced and very good at selling their services. I was excited about building the brand, and that excitement sometimes made me move faster than I should have.

Now, I recommend interviewing at least three to five people or companies before making a significant hire. The interview process itself is an education. You’ll hear different strategies, cost structures and perspectives on what’s possible. Eventually, you’ll begin to recognize who understands the work and who simply knows how to sell it.

And don’t confuse confidence with having all the answers. I started a beverage company at 54 after a career in mental health. I knew a great deal about people and relationships. I knew very little about beverage manufacturing, distribution or retail. That experience has been both humbling and energizing. What I brought into this business wasn’t industry expertise. It was curiosity, conviction and a willingness to learn. I still believe those are some of the most valuable things an entrepreneur can have.

Be ambitious about what you want to build. Just be equally discerning about who you trust to help you build it.
