#5371. Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on AI startup Applied Compute as earnings top forecasts

Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. today announced that it has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence model training and inference startup Applied Compute Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.

The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations. Shares of Palo Alto Networks rose more than 8% in late trading, adding to a gain of nearly 10% during the regular session.

The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter. Once the deal closes, Applied Compute co-founder and Chief Executive Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, with the startup’s research team also joining the company.

Founded in 2025 by former OpenAI Group PBC researchers Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, Applied Compute offers a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models. The platform is designed to make it easier for companies to train, serve and improve their own models, with an autoscaling inference engine and a model router called Shift-1 also included.

Applied Compute raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier this month in a round led by Elad Gil, with Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures and HubSpot Ventures also participating. At the time, the company said that its annualized recurring revenue had topped $100 million. Notable customers include Microsoft Corp. and DoorDash Inc. Coming into its acquisition, Applied Compute had raised more than $500 million in total.

Palo Alto Networks is pitching the deal as a bet that enterprise AI will be hybrid, as a large share of companies run open-weight models tuned to their own data. According to the company, no large provider is currently delivering those models securely. With Applied Compute, enterprises will be able to train and deploy open-weight models with security built in, either in the public cloud or in sovereign environments.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Chairman and Chief Executive Nikesh Arora said. “Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we’ve seen, and its research team is exceptional.”

The deal came on the same day Palo Alto Networks reported what Arora called a record first quarter. For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, the company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.05, up from 93 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 97 cents per share on revenue of $3.31 billion.

Next-generation security annual recurring revenue grew 66% from a year earlier, to $9.73 billion. Remaining performance obligations rose 35%, to $21 billion. Helped by a tax benefit of $457 million, net income on an unadjusted basis came to $482 million, up from $334 million in the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Dipak Golechha said that given the current threat environment and the demand ahead, the company is “materially raising” its full-year guidance.

For its fiscal second quarter, Palo Alto Networks expects adjusted earnings per share of $1.01 to $1.03 on revenue of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion. Full-year revenue is now forecast at $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up from the $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion guided in September, with adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share ahead of the $4.18 expected by analysts polled by FactSet.

#5370. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

#5369. Your Business Is Saving Hours With AI. So Why Are Customers Still Waiting?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Before investing in another automation tool, ask whether the time you’re saving is actually improving your customers’ experience.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

I’ve encountered different versions of this problem throughout my consulting career. Teams have the expertise. The technology exists. Everyone wants to move forward. Yet progress stalls because the underlying process is more complicated than anyone realized.

It made me think about how businesses are approaching artificial intelligence. We’re investing in tools that promise to make work faster, but how often do we stop to examine what’s slowing the business down in the first place?

When entrepreneurs think about productivity, they naturally focus on the time employees spend completing tasks. How quickly can we produce a report? How much time can we save creating content? Can AI respond to routine inquiries? Those are reasonable questions.

But consider what happened in the healthcare project. Automating another task wouldn’t have resolved who owned the account, who could authorize access or how the team should handle authentication. Those were process and accountability problems.

This is why I believe every business should examine its workflows before investing heavily in automation.

I’ve previously written about why entrepreneurs should examine workflows before hiring more employees. The same principle applies to technology.

If responsibilities are unclear and information is scattered, automation may simply help a flawed process move faster.

A business owner might celebrate saving 20 hours a week. The customer is asking a different question: Why am I still waiting?

That gap is easy to overlook because internal performance metrics don’t always reflect the customer experience.

Imagine improving the speed of customer service responses while leaving the underlying resolution process unchanged. Customers might receive answers sooner but still wait days for their problems to be addressed.

The business reports an efficiency improvement. Customers experience little difference. I see a similar disconnect in marketing. Companies sometimes invest in generating more leads without examining what happens after those leads arrive.

As I explored in my article about why businesses can spend more on marketing while attracting fewer customers, more activity doesn’t automatically translate into better commercial results. The lesson applies to AI as well.

Measure the outcome, not just the activity that produced it.

One thing I’ve learned from managing complex projects is that technology cannot replace clear ownership. Someone still needs to make decisions, resolve exceptions and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

Before automating a process, I ask three questions:

If those answers aren’t clear, technology isn’t the first thing I would fix.

For example, automated appointment reminders can reduce administrative effort. But if patients cannot easily reschedule or reach someone when they need help, the experience remains frustrating.

The same is true for sales, onboarding and service delivery. Customers appreciate convenience, but they also want confidence that someone is paying attention.

This may be the most important question entrepreneurs should ask about AI.

Saving time is only valuable when businesses put that time to better use. This is the AI productivity trap: Faster work doesn’t necessarily mean faster growth. The real opportunity lies in using that efficiency to improve customer relationships, solve problems and create measurable business value.

Suppose a new system saves your team 10 hours every week. What do you do with that time? Do you reinvest it in customer relationships? Improve service quality? Reduce expenses? Give employees more opportunities to solve problems that technology cannot handle?

Or does that time simply disappear into additional meetings and administrative work? The answer matters.

In my earlier Entrepreneur article about why business growth doesn’t always improve profitability, I discussed the importance of looking beyond top-line results. Productivity deserves the same scrutiny.

An efficient business isn’t necessarily a profitable one, and a productive team isn’t automatically delivering a better customer experience.

Entrepreneurs need to decide how efficiency gains will create value before assuming they will.

My advice is simple: Choose one process that repeatedly creates problems. It might be customer onboarding, appointment scheduling, account access, proposal approvals or resolving support requests. Follow that process from beginning to end.

Talk to the people involved. Identify where information gets lost, approvals stall or responsibilities become unclear. Then ask whether the problem requires automation at all.

Sometimes the answer is a better system. Sometimes it’s eliminating an unnecessary approval. Sometimes it’s giving one person clear responsibility for following through.

Make one change, measure what happens, and expand what works. You may discover that the most valuable improvement costs considerably less than another software subscription.

I’m enthusiastic about what AI can do for entrepreneurs, especially smaller businesses competing with organizations that have significantly greater resources. But I don’t believe adopting more technology automatically makes a company more competitive.

The healthcare project reinforced something I’ve seen repeatedly: Even capable teams with good technology can struggle when the underlying process isn’t working.

Your customers don’t see how many hours you save internally. They notice whether you deliver what you promised, respond when they need you and make their lives easier.

Before celebrating how much faster your business has become, make sure your customers can feel the difference.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

#5368. ROHM Develops TP-PFC Controller IC for GaN High-frequency Switching

- Enabling High Efficiency and Low Standby Power in Compact AC-DC Power Supplies -

KYOTO, Japan, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ROHM Co., Ltd. has developed a new product known as BM85060FV, a totem-pole power factor correction (TP-PFC) controller IC for high-efficiency, compact AC-DC power supplies. A key feature is its ability to operate in the MHz band, supporting high-frequency switching with GaN HEMTs.

BM85060FV: https://www.rohm.com/products/power-management/ac-dc-converters-ics/ac-dc-converters-ics-pfc/bm85060fv-product

Figures: Product features https://cdn.kyodonewsprwire.jp/prwfile/release/M106254/202611119934/_prw_PI1fl_SCjAGiqn.jpg

As consumer electronics and industrial equipment become more sophisticated, they require more power while also demanding smaller size and higher efficiency. Stricter energy regulations further drive the need for both improved operating efficiency and lower no-load power consumption. GaN HEMTs are gaining adoption due to their high-frequency switching performance.

Additionally, when paired with a bridgeless TP-PFC controller such as BM85060FV, system designers can significantly reduce power loss and solution footprint, enabling compact, high-efficiency power supplies.

This new product enables a system-level efficiency of 99% in 300 to 500 W-class AC-DC power supplies. The high switching frequency allows for the miniaturization of peripheral components, resulting in a smaller solution footprint.

No-load current consumption of 150 microamperes -- a 70% reduction compared to standard products -- makes it easier to reduce system standby power consumption and contributes to the development of power supply systems that meet the energy-saving requirements of DOE Level 7 and CoC Tier 2.

Furthermore, the device incorporates various protection functions required for AC-DC power supplies, including a lightning surge protection circuit, which helps reduce the design burden and improve system reliability.

Sales of the new product began in November 2026. Online sales have also started, and it is available for purchase through online distributors.Online sales: https://www.rohm.com/distribution/-/dinventory/BM85060FV-E2/sample/0

#5367. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:00 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5366. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg, Reuters and the Financial Times, is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.

If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can.

The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks, including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies.

Some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. For instance, both Amazon.com Inc. and Google LLC have sizable stakes in the company, and others including Microsoft Corp., Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. have invested billions into its IPO. Meanwhile, the company is one of the biggest buyers of AI chips from those firms.

“If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei (pictured) said in a roadshow video last week. “We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time.”

Anthropic has been surrounded by immense hype and equally sizable controversy, generating billions of dollars in revenue while raising even more, and sparking serious concerns over the safety of the technology it has pioneered. Amodei has emerged as one of the biggest sources of the numerous doomsday stories surrounding AI, writing essays and repeatedly warning anyone who will listen of the dangers of humans losing control. In addition, he has attracted the ire of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after refusing to let the Pentagon do as it pleases with the company’s tools.

“If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” Amodei wrote in a viral essay in September.

Industry analyst Dan Ives told the New York Post that most investors view Amodei’s comments as “background noise” relative to the growth opportunity Anthropic has as one of the perceived leaders in frontier model development. “It’s a white-knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he said.

Going forward, Amodei and his team will try to defy a stock market that has looked increasingly volatile this year. But even if they fail, they will walk away from this as incredibly rich men, with some reports suggesting that he and his six co-founders could each earn around $18 billion from today’s sale.

“Anthropic’s IPO will test just how much value frontier AI companies can capture as the industry moves from building increasingly capable models to putting them to work,” DatologyAI Inc. CEO Ari Morcos told SiliconANGLE.

Wall Street anticipates massive growth for the company in the coming years. Anthropic has been engaged in a titanic struggle with OpenAI Group PBC and Google LLC to develop the best AI models and recruit enterprise customers, and it appears to be winning, at least for now. It has enjoyed a rapid rise this year driven by the success of its popular AI coding tool Claude Code.

According to its IPO prospectus, it generated revenue of $33.24 billion in the nine month period ending Sept. 30, up about 1,200% from the same period one year earlier. During that period, it recorded a staggering $104 billion net loss, though most of that was the result of a change in the value of convertible notes issues to investors and its derivative liabilities, the Financial Times said. Over the same stretch in 2025, Anthropic’s total losses came to $25.1 billion.

In a recent amendment to its IPO filing, the company said it had achieved a revenue run-rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the prior month.

Regarding projections, some analysts have forecast Anthropic’s revenue to hit $53 billion by the end of its fiscal year, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in fiscal 2027 and between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028.

Anthropic’s rival OpenAI had originally hoped to beat it to the public markets, but its founder and CEO Sam Altman later delayed its listing. Though it has confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, it’s not expected to make its market debut until sometime next year.

#5365. Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5364. Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multistep tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post.

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, but significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

“When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.”

Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the update. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing.

#5363. ‘70% chance’ we’re already in an AI bubble: The economist who said ‘not yet’ in January now sees all four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse

Owen Lamont told Fortune in January that the stock market wasn’t in an AI bubble. Now he’s mostly convinced.

“I think there is a 70% chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the U.S. stock market,” Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and a former University of Chicago finance professor, told Fortune in an email. “I think a lot has changed this year.”

What changed is the one signal he used to say was missing. Lamont tracks what he calls the “four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse”: overvaluation, bubble beliefs, issuance and inflows of new money. At the time, he said three were present. The holdout was issuance, meaning companies selling new stock to the public. Back then, U.S. firms had bought back roughly $1 trillion of their own shares over the past year, and Lamont treats corporate executives as the “smart money.” They weren’t selling.

They are now. U.S. companies issued a net $2.4 trillion of stock over the 12 months to Nov. 12, by Lamont’s count. In the 12 months to November 2025, they bought back a net $69 billion, and a year before that, $397 billion. In his latest Owenomics blog post, he walks back his January headline: “Today, I would no longer write those words.”

“I think we basically have all four horsemen now,” he told Fortune.

The big number has a big asterisk. Of the $2.4 trillion issuance, $2.2 trillion comes from SpaceX’s June IPO, which Lamont’s method counts at its full market value. Strip it out and net issuance is $192 billion.

That’s still a reversal from net buybacks a year earlier, and the turn includes the biggest names: the Magnificent Seven went from net buybacks of $144 billion in the year to November 2024 to net issuance of $276 billion now, according to Lamont. He writes that Alphabet and Meta switched from buying back shares to issuing them, Tesla sharply increased issuance, and Meta announced plans to raise nearly $98 billion in equity to fund its AI spending.

Lamont admits the SpaceX question is “tough.” “I think one company is not enough to constitute a ‘wave of issuance,’” he said. “On the other hand, we live in a world of concentrated stock markets where a handful of companies have huge market cap, so maybe we should expect waves of issuance that are also concentrated.”

Professional investors are moving the other way: fund managers just cut their net overweight in tech to 12% from 37%, the biggest one-month drop since June 2006, according to Bank of America’s November survey.

Why companies are selling is the open question. In his note, Lamont laid out two explanations: “the smart money is selling because the market is overpriced,” or firms “need to fund the AI buildout.” Asked which he leans toward, he said: “I’m not sure. Could be both.”

Either way, the shares are going to someone. TD Securities’ rates strategists flagged the same shift from the bond side this week, noting that Meta and Oracle have issued equity and that more AI capex funded with stock could ease pressure on long-term Treasury yields.

He also thinks the case for overvaluation got stronger this year because real long-term interest rates rose about 100 basis points. But he isn’t calling a top. “It is not a slam dunk case: the market might be overvalued, but it is not absurdly overvalued,” he said. “Net issuance has turned positive, but it’s not strongly positive.”

By his measure, net issuance is running at 3.1% of total market value, still below the peaks of the 1999–2000 tech bubble and the 2021 COVID boom.

Lamont gave Fortune three conditions that would take him from 70% to a flat call.

“First, the Anthropic IPO occurs and is a success. Second, we see a wave of smaller IPOs, similar to what we saw in 2021: hundreds of IPOs, say five IPOs a week, many of them doubling on the first day. Third, CAPE ratio or other valuation ratios blow through prior records.”

The second one is far off. The U.S. had 90 IPOs in 2025, against 311 in 2021 and 677 in 1996, according to Jay Ritter’s data cited in Lamont’s March note. In January, he told Fortune the shortage of IPOs was “baffling,” and that a full bubble could look like the Nasdaq 100 doubling in a year with the Shiller CAPE ratio near 80. It was around 40 then.

The first condition is about a day away. Anthropic is set to price its IPO Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Lamont writes that the deal, if it goes ahead, would push issuance above its 2021 peak. Asked if that’s the moment to watch, he said yes, and pointed back to his three conditions.

#5362. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

#5361. Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck

High-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery.

That shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC.

“We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver said.

Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. (* Disclosure below.)

Google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The company laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements. Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik.

“You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.”

Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up front to decide which candidates are worth testing, Ma-Weaver noted.

“What we’re seeing, for example, with computer-aided engineering, is that you can actually identify ahead of time which are non-essential parameters and you don’t run the simulation, thereby reducing the total simulation time,” she said. “We also find that if you’re doing design and you have initial prototypes, you can generate new, novel and creative prototypes.”

The gains are already reaching weather forecasting in production. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s forecasting platform has heavy, tightly coupled workloads and once ran only on-premises, but it now runs on Google Cloud, Ma-Weaver explained. The National Hurricane Center also used Google’s WeatherNext model to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, Gawlik noted. But the growing reliance on AI-generated results also carries a risk for younger researchers, who may lean on machine output instead of developing critical-thinking skills, she added.

“AI is still not perfect,” Gawlik said. “I think even though there’s an output, we call it AI slop. It could still be slop.”

#5360. Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians

As AI forces office workers to rethink how tasks get done, skilled trades jobs have largely been seen as a more insulated, safer path to a six-figure career. However, hands-on roles like plumbers, electricians, and auto technicians aren’t exactly immune to the changes sweeping the workforce, either.

“Nothing is future-proof,” Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday. “But I do think that a lot of the skilled trades are just those jobs that are going to be required to have a human there.”

Auto technicians—who are in short supply, for example —could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, she said, but still need a human to do the actual manual labor.

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard echoed that AI-powered efficiency will change how skilled trades workers do their jobs—but she said that the industry’s labor needs—fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments—will continue to outpace any productivity gains from the technology.

“No matter how good we get at encouraging people, I think we’re always going to be challenged to get the number of people that we need into the trades to just rebuild the infrastructure of the country,” Hubbard said on stage in an interview with Fortune’s Kristin Stoller.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034—but roughly a quarter of the industry’s existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement.

Skilled trades work isn’t for everyone. The jobs can be physically demanding, require working outdoors in difficult conditions, and sometimes depend on project availability. But they can also offer something increasingly attractive to workers: relatively strong job security, salaries that can reach six figures, and even a pathway to owning a business.

Getting more people to recognize those opportunities, however, has been a challenge.

“We’re seeing pushback both on the cost of college, what jobs really require college degrees,” said Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future. But decades of trade policies and other economic shifts have also left some communities with fewer skilled trades opportunities than they once had, she said.

“We’re having to rebuild trust, rebuild that awareness, and helping parents, young people, school counselors really understand what these 124 different skilled trades occupations offer and what the paths are into those roles,” Flynn said.

That perception gap is particularly evident among the people responsible for advising students on their next steps. While 95% of counselors agree trade school is a valuable and credible post-high school option, just 54% say they often recommend vocational or trade school, and only 28% often recommend an apprenticeship, according to a report released earlier this year by the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades.

“We need to change the perception and get the guidance counselors to start talking about the opportunities,” Culler said.

Even after convincing someone that a skilled trades career might be right for them, the industry still has to get them through the training process and into a job.

The Alliance’s September report found that among every 100 who start an apprenticeship, just 48 complete the program, and only 29 enter a skilled trade occupation within five years of leaving it. The numbers are similarly challenging for related postsecondary programs: Of every 100 entrants, 48 complete their programs and just 34 go on to work in a skilled trade.

Flynn described the problem as “pipeline leakiness,” which can often come down to a lack of support for workers navigating training programs. That includes seemingly basic but consequential barriers like transportation and childcare.

“We really need to be working on this together,” she said.

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5359. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

#5358. Bitcoin Price Holds $64K Ahead of Nvidia Earnings: AI Bubble Finally Pops?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

This timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Big Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

His argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

This accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

The concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

Burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

“Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman said.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

The disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an important historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

The shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

An AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

Investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The company’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an important technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former company built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?

#5357. Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices

When Chipotle overhauled its rewards program in April, it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices.

For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported.

“I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel moderated by this reporter.

Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500, Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math.

Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards.

“We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me with 10 ideas on how to increase value for the consumer and let’s have a conversation.”

That stance tracks with Chipotle’s refusal to chase traffic with deep discounts. In February, Boatwright said he didn’t want to “devalue our core offering” with McDonald’s-style deals and planned price increases below the rate of inflation. Loyalty perks let the chain hand its most frequent diners more value without cutting menu prices for everyone.

The same logic shaped Chipotle’s answer to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs: a high-protein menu with low-priced add-ons rather than markdowns. “You’ve got to have innovation that doesn’t discount the core offering, but meets a consumer need state,” Boatwright said.

Spring, who took over as CEO of Macy’s Inc. in February 2024, has been steering the 168-year-old department store operator’s turnaround. He said a loyalty program only works if shoppers believe it does.

“Loyalty is integral, I think, to the relationships people have with brands,” Spring said. “And we are constantly striving at Macy’s, Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury to make sure that the loyalty program has value in the eyes of the consumer, not in our eyes.”

The payoff comes when a shopper decides where to look first, at the mall or online. “If the Macy’s app or the Bloomingdale’s app is there and I already have rewards in my wallet, it’s going to encourage me to go there maybe and complete my activity,” he said.

Macy’s program is built to be easy to join, Spring said, with rewards that don’t depend on how a customer pays and bigger ones for Macy’s credit card holders. The most committed shoppers can earn perks like free merchandise, free delivery, and after-hours shopping. “If you are more committed to us, we want to provide that value to you,” he said.

Spring is also thinking about what happens to those perks when an AI agent does the shopping. Macy’s has started working with Google’s Gemini on agentic commerce, he said, and the priority is making sure reward points, gift cards, and delivery promises still work when a bot places the order.

Food, clothes, and home goods offer sensory experiences that financial services can’t match, and few people feel much affection for their bank. Ally Financial, which bills itself as the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., is trying anyway. In May, it rolled out Loyally, a fee-free rewards program open to customers regardless of their account balance.

“The question really is how can we add some real value for customers that gives them reasons they want to keep on coming back to our site and engaging with us,” Rhodes said. “We’ve literally had it for like six months now, but the early results are really encouraging.”

Ally is starting from a strong base, by Rhodes’ account. He said customer retention runs well over 90%, about 15% of new account volume comes through referrals, and 70% of customers are Gen Z or millennials.

Rhodes argued that AI search is raising the stakes on every customer interaction, because what customers and employees say about a brand feeds the engines that make recommendations. “There are people who spend 10 times what we spend,” he said of Ally’s marketing budget. “Yet in the AI search engines and unbranded inquiries in consumer banking, we show up number one.”

The harder balance is rewarding regulars while still persuading new customers to try a brand. Spring said that’s where a retailer’s customer data comes in: breaking shoppers into cohorts and targeting each one, both to drive new traffic and to “create extraordinary value for your highest, most loyal consumers.”

“It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach,” Spring said. “It needs to be very bespoke. And you have to leverage tools like, dare I say, AI.”

Boatwright said every change to Chipotle’s program aims to draw more users in at the top of the funnel, then “make it much more sticky within the funnel and get those consumers coming back more often.”

The next test may come when the customer isn’t the one searching. Boatwright said agentic AI ordering is coming whether brands are ready or not, and Chipotle has to make sure it shows up “when you ask your agent, tell me the best burrito in town.”

Phil Wahba is a senior writer at Fortune primarily focused on leadership coverage, with a prior focus on retail.

#5356. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.
