#5340. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#5339. Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation

Anthropic priced shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above its initially guided ranged of $70 to $78 per share, and valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic’s stock will begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ANT, marking one of the most highly anticipated IPOs in years as well as one of the largest ever.

The San Francisco-based AI company said Wednesday that it increased the number of shares sold in the offering to 980 million, instead of the 825 million shares it initially indicated it would sell. The expanded float means Anthropic will raise roughly $79.4 billion in the IPO—and as much as $91.6 billion if the deal’s underwriters choose to exercise an over-allotment option.

The IPO will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic in San Francisco just five years ago. Some—including CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniella Amodei, and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan—are cashing in small portions of their equity through the offering, with existing shareholders selling 23.6 million shares.

At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion would top the $75 billon raised by SpaceX.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price—meaning that, all told, Anthropic could exit the deal with proceeds of $118 billion.

The high share price straight out of the gates will put immense pressure on Anthropic as it seeks to justify its valuation to investors and to prove that AI tools can deliver the massive payoff Wall Street expects.

Anticipation for the IPOs of Anthropic and its arch-rival OpenAI has been building ever since OpenAI ignited the generative AI boom in late 2022 with the launch of ChatGPT. With OpenAI holding off on its IPO until at least 2027, Anthropic becomes the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also does rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media).

Anthropic’s Wall Street debut is being closely watched as a barometer for the health of the broader AI industry. The IPO comes as the AI boom is in a period of uncertainty following a leadership shake up at AI chipmaker Nvidia and growing public backlash to AI data centers. High profile incidents of rogue AI agents, by OpenAI as well as Anthropic, have added to the unease over the technology.

“I think if we do this right we can create an age of miracles, where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” said Amodei, the CEO, in a video the company posted online for its IPO investor roadshow.

Amodei, once the VP of research at OpenAI, left to cofound Anthropic at the end of 2020, along with sister Daniella and several other OpenAI employees, when they became disillusioned with OpenAI’s approach to AI safety. Still, the company’s IPO prospectus is replete with warnings of the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers, a market in which Anthropic has been especially successfull. In the nine months ending September 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.

“Anthropic will need to sustain rapid growth while managing the enormous cost of developing and running its models, and there is still considerable uncertainty around how the competitive landscape and economics of generative AI will evolve,” said Morningstar analyst Malik Ahmed Khan in an emailed statement on Wednesday.

Despite the risks, and the already massive valuation for a newly public company, Khan said he believed Anthropic’s fair value is actually closer to $92 per share. “Our valuation reflects the significant growth we expect from AI adoption and Anthropic’s position at the frontier of model development, particularly in areas such as coding and cybersecurity,” Khan said.

When the stock begins trading, likely around midday on Thursday, investors will finally have their chance to opine on the “fair” share price.

Alexei Oreskovic is the Tech editor at Fortune.

#5338. How to Spot Employee Burnout Before the Holiday Rush Takes Its Toll

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s how small businesses can use workforce technology to prevent employee burnout and keep operations running smoothly.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

The right workforce technology helps owners see that pressure building. Connecting scheduling, timekeeping and payroll information makes it possible to spot recurring workload problems, understand who is affected and adjust coverage before another request to stay late becomes the only solution.

UKG’s 2025 Retail Workforce Report found that only 18% of retailers anticipated employee burnout as a major challenge. Meanwhile, UKG’s 2025 global study of frontline workers found that 76% of frontline employees reported feeling burned out at work.

Underestimating that strain can lead an owner to plan for holiday sales the team cannot sustainably support. If the staffing plan assumes everyone can keep adding hours, a single absence can leave the business struggling to serve customers and put even more pressure on the people who remain. Earlier visibility into workload gives owners time to arrange coverage before that cycle begins.

Small business leaders often work alongside their employees and know them well. Yet familiarity can make a staffing problem harder to recognize. The person who always volunteers becomes the first person asked, and a supervisor’s willingness to stay late gradually becomes part of the plan.

Disconnected systems make that pattern easier to miss. A schedule shows a filled shift, while payroll records the extra hours after they have been worked. Bringing those records together gives owners a clearer view of how often the business depends on the same employees to close its staffing gaps.

Overtime is one of the most important workforce operations signals because it shows where demand and workforce capacity are no longer aligned. Occasional extra hours may be welcome for some, but repeated overtime concentrated among a few employees warrants a closer look, especially when their schedules also leave little time between shifts.

Imagine a small retailer whose most experienced associate regularly stays an hour past her scheduled finish. Each request seems reasonable in isolation. Over three weeks, however, she also covers two absences and works several closing shifts followed by early openings. The owner sees someone dependable; the combined records reveal the true cost of how much additional work she is carrying.

Connected timekeeping and scheduling tools can make that cumulative demand visible without requiring the owner to reconstruct it from old schedules and messages. Alerts about approaching overtime or short intervals between shifts give a manager a chance to discuss coverage before publishing the next schedule.

Attendance changes add another piece of context. If absences rise on a team that has been working extra hours, the combination is worth exploring. While data alone does not establish that someone is burned out, it helps managers ask better questions about workload and support.

This is where workforce analytics earns its value for a lean business: It helps owners manage workforce operations proactively rather than reactively. Effective workforce operations requires connecting labor demand, staffing levels, scheduling, attendance, timekeeping and employee experience data to create a complete picture of how work gets done. When leaders can see those connections, they can intervene before a staffing challenge becomes an operational disruption.

Holiday staffing decisions often start with last year’s sales, but sales alone cannot explain why a team keeps falling behind. A store may have enough labor hours for the week and still depend on employees staying late because coverage does not line up with the work. That mismatch can turn an otherwise manageable holiday workload into a recurring source of exhaustion.

Consider a shop where afternoon pickup orders regularly arrive while employees are unloading a delivery. Associates leave stocking unfinished to help customers, then spend the end of their shifts catching up. To an owner reviewing weekly totals, the overtime may suggest the store simply needs more hours overall. Connecting order activity, labor demand, scheduling and timekeeping data can reveal a workforce operations problem that would otherwise remain hidden.

With demand forecasting and scheduling technology, that pattern can inform the next schedule. If the overlap is likely to recur, the manager can plan for stockroom coverage while keeping associates available to serve customers. AI-assisted scheduling can help identify an employee with the right skills and availability, reducing the time the manager spends working through possible changes.

The benefit is that the closing team no longer has to absorb the same unfinished work night after night. Addressing the bottleneck earlier can make finishing on time more predictable, giving employees greater confidence in their schedules. For the owner, it also creates a clearer basis for deciding whether to move existing coverage or invest in additional hours.

Better data also makes employee conversations more useful. A manager who can see repeated extra shifts can ask how that arrangement is working and what would make the coming weeks manageable. The answer may be a consistent day off, a different start time or continued access to additional hours.

That distinction matters during a season when employees may be balancing holiday expenses with family responsibilities. An automatic reduction in hours could create a different source of stress. Current availability and employee preferences help managers respond to what people actually need.

In UKG’s 2025 retail survey, 86% of retailers said frontline employees wanted more flexibility than their organizations provided. For small businesses, delivering that flexibility can be difficult when every change requires phone calls, group texts and a manager to coordinate the exchange.

Mobile self-service scheduling reduces that friction by letting employees view schedules, request time off and arrange shift swaps in one place. Scheduling rules can help check that replacement coverage meets role requirements and flag potential overtime. Employees gain a practical way to manage a conflict, while managers spend less time chasing responses.

The benefit goes beyond convenience. Someone who can resolve a scheduling conflict has more control over how work fits into life outside it. When employees see that technology makes those adjustments easier, they have a concrete reason to trust its role in the workplace.

Small businesses rarely have someone available to spend hours analyzing workforce reports. Technology is more useful when it brings a developing problem to the manager’s attention and makes the next decision easier, such as highlighting an open shift alongside qualified employees who are available to work.

Timing determines how many options remain. A coverage gap identified before next week’s schedule is published may be addressed through a voluntary shift change or additional staffing. The same gap discovered during a rush is more likely to land on whoever is already there.

Managers need that support themselves. UKG’s retail report found that 31% of retailers said managers worked additional shifts when understaffed. A supervisor covering the floor has less time to plan coverage or help a new employee learn the job, which can leave the team dependent on the same experienced people again.

Keeping demand forecasts and schedules connected also matters after peak sales pass. Returns and inventory work can continue into January, and a smaller team may still face a substantial workload. Visibility into that work gives owners a better basis for deciding when staffing can ease.

A successful holiday season depends on having a workforce that can sustain the work and the operational visibility to support it. Burnout, absenteeism, overtime, scheduling conflicts and staffing shortages are often treated as separate challenges, but they are all connected workforce operations signals.

When small businesses bring those signals together, they gain a clearer understanding of how work gets done across the organization. Workforce operations technology provides the visibility needed to identify strain early, align staffing with demand and respond before employee pressure becomes an operational problem.

Ultimately, organizations that manage workforce operations effectively are better positioned to support their people, serve customers consistently and perform through the busiest times of the year.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

#5337. ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think

Many people are understandably shaken after a string of nationwide outages over the past week—from flights being grounded, to emails not coming through, bank transactions failing, and much more—with no clear explanation from politicians or businesses about what exactly happened.

One thing officials have made clear is that the outages are not a result of a coordinated cyberattack, quelling fears that AI may have empowered bad actors to take down critical systems. However, AI still appears to have played a significant, if unexpected, role. Advanced AI models are speeding up the discovery of software vulnerabilities, which tech teams are racing to patch before bad actors can exploit them with equally powerful AI tools.

The botched implementation of those patches was linked to an outage earlier this week of an internal communications system at the National Security Agency (NSA), as well as the “banking outages,” a spokesperson for Senator Mark Warner’s team told Fortune. Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and JPMorgan Chase all suffered outages this week.

“It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said in a statement. The Washington Sun also reported that bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches were to blame for the service disruptions.

The irony is that the tools aimed at preventing system outages seem to be causing them, or at least influencing new forms of human error. Bank of America disclosed last month it had hired 1,000 contractors to patch flaws exposed by Anthropic’s Mythos model, on top of 3,000 internal staffers, CNBC reported. That does not mean businesses should abandon AI-powered defensive cybersecurity tools, but rather suggests that their implementation is not going according to plan.

“This is a failure of implementation,” Amit Shah, founder and CEO of InstaLILY AI, tells Fortune. “The AI finds a vulnerability in seconds and may not know what else breaks when you fix it. The person approving the patch sees a recommendation, not the systems it touches. So a tool built to prevent outages can end up causing them.”

Anxiety around “the theoretical risk of a breach” is prompting a “rush to eliminate” vulnerabilities, Jeff Collins, CEO of the IT technology platform WanAware, tells Fortune. “AI now discovers vulnerabilities at machine speed while our testing and deployment safeguards remain stuck at human speed.”

Thanks to AI tools’ thoroughness, IT teams are overwhelmed with fixes to implement, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said on X. “Some of the recent outages are a consequence of a deluge of patches,” Arora said. Between these teams’ mandates to plug holes, and the threat of “AI-assisted hacks, we have a challenge,” Arora said, with “no silver bullets.”

“The issue is that the volume of issues we’re fixing is so large that it’s pressuring our staff to apply large amounts of fixes that can break things,” Cliff Steinhauer, Director of Information Security & Engagement, National Cybersecurity Alliance tells Fortune. “We don’t always have time to fully test every update because there are so many and attackers can pick up the known vulnerabilities and exploit them.”

But Steinhauer doesn’t consider this an implementation failure. Instead, he sees it as a necessary phase enterprises must go through as they secure their code bases. “I think we are in a bell curve of vulnerabilities discovery and patching. The hope is that we’ll get to a peak, then it will start to descend and slow down once we start to fix the underlying issues in our software.” He compares it to road maintenance. If the Department of Transportation (DOT) “finds a crack in the bridge, they have to shut down traffic to fix it, which is disruptive. But if the bridge collapses, that’s obviously worse.”

The onus of responsibility between the human and the AI remains hard to pin down. While the human may not have properly vetted the impact of the fixes, it’s unclear what information they were operating on from the AI tool. Did the AI create anxiety by overstating the vulnerabilities’ significance? Did it recommend changes en masse, that perhaps a human approved without proper vetting? Are security team managers pushing teams to embrace AI as fast as possible, to avoid a potentially catastrophic breach?

“The failure isn’t that AI patches too aggressively or that exhausted engineers rubber-stamp fixes, but that we plugged a hyper fast diagnostic engine into legacy operational pipelines never built to absorb that velocity of change,” Collins said.

OpenAI offers cybersecurity-specific models to help organizations find vulnerabilities at scale, and is rapidly enrolling new customers to its Daybreak program that provides approved security professionals with its most powerful defensive cyber tools. The goal is to “patch the planet,” as OpenAI has named its Daybreak initiative to secure code better than ever before. Its Daybreak products include dashboards that classify bugs by severity and aim to help teams triage them. Anthropic’s version of Daybreak is called Project Glasswing.

A week and a half before its outage, on Nov. 5, OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman announced a partnership with JPMorgan Chase to use OpenAI models to help secure its systems.

A JPMorgan Chase spokesperson said OpenAI’s tools were not a factor in the outage. The spokesperson said the problem traced back to “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.” The spokesperson added that the company did not identify that bug through AI tools or fix it with AI.

OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman recently told The Information there was “no question” that cyber would eventually become a bigger business for the company than coding. The company swapped out its Chief Revenue Officer earlier this year for Dali Rajic, and tasked him with leveraging his cybersecurity enterprise sales experience to accelerate that business line.

The widespread adoption of AI tools for defensive cybersecurity might be trickier than these organizations initially expected. Plus, lawmakers are seizing on the recent outages to demand more patch-related guardrails. Representative Andy Ogle plans to introduce legislation today that calls for better coordination as AI speeds up the discovery and exploitation of software flaws, NextGov reports.

#5336. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

#5335. If Indonesia wants 8% growth, it needs to give investors confidence that contracts won’t change on them

Indonesia faces a test of investor confidence. A volatile stretch for the stock market, pressure on the rupiah, and concerns over fiscal discipline and policy uncertainty have raised questions about the direction of Southeast Asia’s largest economy—questions sharpened by MSCI’s proposal to reclassify Indonesian equities to “standalone” status, outside the benchmark emerging-market indexes that guide global portfolios.

Yet despite these wobbles, the long-term investment case for Indonesia remains strong. I saw it firsthand in Jakarta, where I recently led a business delegation of 33 American companies—investors, employers, and partners in developing Indonesia’s workforce. Across engagements with senior government officials and business leaders, one takeaway was clear: The U.S. business community remains committed to the Indonesian market.

But confidence cannot be taken for granted.

President Prabowo Subianto has set an ambitious target of 8% economic growth by 2029. Indonesia’s economy expanded 5.47% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, and the government is targeting 6% growth in 2027. Indonesia has the resources, talent, and market to pursue these ambitions. The challenge is creating the conditions that turn that potential into sustained investment.

Our discussions reinforced a simple point: Indonesia’s next wave of investment need not come only from new entrants. It can come from companies already operating there—businesses that have built factories, developed suppliers, trained workers, and established deep roots in the economy.

The question is what will encourage them to expand.

First, investors need confidence in the rules. Businesses can manage commercial risk. What they cannot easily manage is uncertainty over whether established agreements will be honored or regulations applied consistently. Concerns over changes to existing contractual terms and shifting regulatory requirements have unsettled investors in several sectors. Predictability, consistency, and fair treatment are fundamental to long-term investment decisions.

Energy offers a clear example. Indonesia wants to boost domestic production and strengthen energy security. American oil and gas companies have long supported these goals, helping meet domestic energy needs, develop local capabilities, and strengthen Indonesia’s competitiveness in global energy markets. These investments are made over decades, not quarters. Indonesia’s broader push for greater national control over natural resources has raised questions about the long-term security of investments. In oil and gas, regulations allowing changes to production-sharing contracts, including cost recovery and tax provisions, illustrate why contractual certainty remains an important issue. Sustaining this partnership requires respect for the agreements already signed.

This principle is widely recognized. The OECD, which Indonesia aspires to join, emphasizes the sanctity of contracts and the importance of parties fulfilling their obligations. The World Bank’s Business Ready framework puts a similar premium on reliable contract enforcement.

The new Oil and Gas Bill, currently under consideration in Parliament, offers an opportunity to strengthen that confidence. The proposed legislation would overhaul the management of upstream oil and gas operations and clarify certain investment provisions. Ensuring that the final law protects existing commitments, provides competitive fiscal terms, and improves regulatory certainty would help unlock investment in domestic production. Expanded U.S.-Indonesia energy cooperation could also strengthen supply security and deepen our economic partnership.

The principle extends well beyond energy. In manufacturing, changes to import licensing requirements have previously left thousands of containers stranded at Indonesian ports, disrupting access to essential materials and components. In technology, overlapping data localization requirements and evolving rules for cross-border data transfers can complicate investment in cloud infrastructure and digital services. These uncertainties carry real costs. Predictable policies give companies the confidence to plan, invest, and grow.

Second, Indonesia must make it easier to do business. Capital is mobile. Across Southeast Asia, governments are competing to attract investment, develop industries, and create skilled jobs. Indonesia cannot rely on the size of its market alone.

Consider manufacturing. Companies need timely access to equipment, components, and materials that may not yet be available domestically. Delays at the border can stall production and raise costs. In healthcare, duplicative testing and certification requirements can slow access to medicines and medical technology. While these regulations serve legitimate goals, including safety and quality assurance, requirements that duplicate internationally recognized standards without improving outcomes impose avoidable costs. Removing such barriers would benefit Indonesian businesses and consumers as much as foreign investors.

Equally important is meaningful consultation with the private sector before major laws and regulations are introduced. That means engaging businesses early, allowing adequate time to review proposals, and incorporating practical industry feedback before rules are finalized. Such dialogue can help policymakers anticipate unintended consequences, improve implementation, and give investors greater certainty.

Third, investment must build Indonesia’s own capabilities. President Prabowo’s emphasis on strengthening domestic industry is an objective American businesses share. The most successful investments create opportunities well beyond the companies making them.

Strengthening domestic industry also requires access to foreign technology, equipment, and materials that cannot yet be produced competitively at home. Local content requirements that exceed domestic production capacity can delay projects. A more effective approach would pair realistic requirements with supplier development, workforce training, and technology transfer.

The digital economy offers another opportunity. Clear, practical rules for artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and cybersecurity can help Indonesian businesses adopt new technologies, improve productivity, and create skilled jobs. American companies can be partners in that transformation.

These are not competing priorities. A stronger investment climate and a stronger domestic economy go hand in hand.

I left Jakarta encouraged by the government’s willingness to engage and its determination to deliver economic growth. But the real measure of progress will be what follows those discussions. Dialogue matters. Implementation matters more.

Indonesia’s recent challenges underscore the importance of that work. Market confidence can be fragile, and political uncertainty carries economic costs. Investors are watching not just Indonesia’s growth prospects, but the consistency and credibility of its economic policies as well.

American companies are not short-term speculators. We are long-term investors and partners. Our commitment to Indonesia has endured through economic downturns and political transitions. We intend to build on it.

Indonesia does not need to convince us of its potential. We already believe in it. The opportunity now is to translate that belief into more investment, more jobs, and lasting prosperity for the Indonesian people. That begins with a simple principle: consistent and fair treatment of investors, backed by policies they can trust and commitments they can count on.

#5334. Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share, raising a record $81 billion in biggest offering ever

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Claude maker's stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the symbol ANT after pricing above its $70 to $78 range

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, and shares of its Class A common stock were set to debut on the Nasdaq $NDAQ on Thursday with the symbol "ANT."

The offering totals $81 billion, edging past the $75 billion that SpaceX collected when it went public in Junel. SpaceX's total reached $85.7 billion after its underwriters exercised their overallotment option, according to CNBC. Anthropic has given its underwriters a 30-day option to buy up to 147,000,000 more of its Class A common stock.

The offering totals 980,000,000 Class A common stock, of which Anthropic is selling 956,351,354 and certain selling stockholders are selling 23,648,646, the company said. Anthropic receives no proceeds from the selling stockholders' portion. The offering is expected to close on Nov. 20, subject to customary closing conditions.

The price tops the $70 to $78 range Anthropic had guided for a planned offering of 825 million, according to The Wall Street Journal. Investors asked to buy several times as much stock as Anthropic put up for sale. The offering should put Anthropic's fully diluted valuation at roughly $1.5 trillion.

Goldman Sachs $GS and Morgan Stanley $MS are the contacts listed for copies of the final prospectus, which the company said is the only means by which the offering is being made.

Amazon $AMZN and Google $GOOGL are set to own about 28% of Anthropic in aggregate after the IPO and a concurrent private placement of about $26 billion. Microsoft $MSFT and Google are among seven companies that agreed to buy non-voting Class N stock in that placement at the IPO price. The purchase depends on the IPO being completed.

New York City Comptroller Mark Levine has criticized Anthropic's governance plans for the offering and urged the company in an Oct. 14 letter to pause the IPO. Anthropic's filing lists a single share of Class F stock held by a founders' entity that carries 50.1% of total voting power. Anthropic will be a controlled company under Nasdaq rules, and its seven co-founders, together with an independent trust, will remain in charge after the listing.

#5333. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5332. The Rooms Where AI Gets Decided Are Filling Up. Women Need to Be in Them

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is redrawing the path to leadership within companies, and women risk being left out. Proximity to the AI strategy, governance, and operating decisions that guide the next generation of enterprise leadership is critical for women looking to grow their career, expand their role, or become leaders in their organization.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

AI is one of the biggest market-moving shifts we have ever seen. Leaders are reorganizing around the technology, new businesses are being built around the opportunity, and decisions being made about AI today will define our economy for generations.

I care passionately about seeing more women in leadership, having access to capital, and steering the choices that shape our world. So when I heard AI expert and advisor Allie K. Miller on Emma Grede’s podcast share that women were adopting AI 25% less than men, it stuck with me.

For my whole career, I’ve watched women start a step behind: we still hold only about 29% of C-suite roles and make up fewer than one in five decision-makers at venture firms. Even 2025, a banner year for women-founded startups, tells a misleading story: nearly 41% of the almost $74 billion raised came from two megadeals. Most women founders saw very few of those investment dollars.If women are already underrepresented among leaders, investors, and founders, and now we’re adopting AI more slowly, the gap widens at the exact moment the next generation of business leaders and global decision-makers are being decided.

Concerns around whether AI is ethical or looks like cheating are driving women’s slower adoption, but I also think it comes down to time. We badly underestimate what it takes to carve out hours to learn something new on top of a full-time job, personal responsibilities, and commitments to friends and loved ones. If I spend a Sunday afternoon building an agent, I’m missing time with my family. The trade-offs are real, and you don’t get that time back.

Research suggests the adoption gap may be shrinking, but given how fast AI is moving, incremental progress is not enough. This isn’t a shift women can opt out of. If we want to drive the decisions that will define the next decade, we need to be leading this transformation, not watch it unfold.Here are four things I believe women should focus on right now:

I always come back to this line from Ginni Rometty: growth and comfort do not coexist.I’ve seen this firsthand throughout my career: I joined ServiceNow just before COVID hit. Within ten weeks, I went from never having worked from home to doing everything remotely—building relationships, leading a team, and learning dozens of new tools. It wasn’t comfortable, but my team and I adapted. AI demands the same mindset.

The women I see pulling ahead here are the ones who just start using AI before they feel ready or have it all figured out. Getting your hands dirty is the whole point: use AI to analyze a dense report, pressure-test a strategy, or build a simple agent to handle a task you dislike.Pick low-risk moments and let yourself get things wrong. You learn AI by being close to it, not by watching from a distance and waiting until you feel like an expert.

You don’t have to navigate this shift alone. Seek out AI-specific meetups and groups—and connect with professionals who are experimenting in real time and asking the same questions as you.

It is also worth looking closer to home. Some of our best AI teachers at ServiceNow have been early-career employees who are more comfortable with these tools than others. A little reverse mentoring can go a long way.

Just as importantly, you need to pay it forward. The more women help each other build confidence and capability around AI, the faster we will close the gap. One of the reasons we invited Allie K. Miller to talk about AI and leadership at Knowledge, our annual conference, is that she consistently shares insights that lower the barrier to entry for others.

You can’t be what you can’t see, which is why those of us in senior leadership roles also need to lead by example. When I’m asked how I use AI as a CFO, I’m deliberate about sharing how it has become a real partner in how I work. I want women coming up behind me to see AI fluency as part of their own leadership path, too.

For much of my career, I was the only woman with a seat at the table. Looking back, I can see how much that proximity shaped my career. Watching leaders like Barry Diller and Dara Khosrowshahi navigate complex, high-stakes decisions taught me lessons no class ever could.It also gave me exposure to projects that prepared me to lead. Before IAC, I didn’t have much M&A experience. There, I learned what a good deal actually looks like, how to think about integration, and the kind of judgment you can only build by doing the work.

The same principle applies to women and AI right now. Get as close to the AI decision-making as possible. Participate in strategy conversations, use-case assessments, pilots, and learning sessions. Raise your hand for the AI project no one has figured out yet and ask to be in the room where your company is determining how it will use this technology.

When leadership sees you leaning into the hardest, most important work the company is taking on, you become someone they picture in the next big role.

Understand Your Role in the AI TransformationWe need more than just engineers and programmers working closely with AI.

To ensure artificial intelligence is as safe, ethical, and effective as it can be, we need people with diverse perspectives and skills working on it. Those with expertise in governance, risk, talent, and change management, for example, have important roles to play in ensuring successful AI deployment at scale.

At ServiceNow, when we added “AI Enablement” to Jacqui Canney’s title of Chief People Officer, it was done for a reason. AI can’t just be dropped into the tooling mix. People need to understand and learn how to use it well in the enterprise, which means we need to invest in that happening.

We’ve done this in many ways, from company-wide learning sessions, to role-based skills development opportunities through ServiceNow University, to building groups of AI champions that shape how the technology is being used at the team level.

Even the best company programs won’t do it all for you, though. I always say that no one will care as much about your career as you do, and that’s to no fault of your managers or your company. They may open doors, but you’re the one who must walk through them.

The rooms where AI is being built, deployed, trained, and governed are filling up, and if you’re not in them, those decisions are getting made without you. The time you invest now in learning, the skills you build, and the judgment you develop will compound. As this next era of leadership unfolds, the women who stayed close to AI won’t just be ready for the future; they’ll help define it.

AI is one of the biggest market-moving shifts we have ever seen. Leaders are reorganizing around the technology, new businesses are being built around the opportunity, and decisions being made about AI today will define our economy for generations.

I care passionately about seeing more women in leadership, having access to capital, and steering the choices that shape our world. So when I heard AI expert and advisor Allie K. Miller on Emma Grede’s podcast share that women were adopting AI 25% less than men, it stuck with me.

For my whole career, I’ve watched women start a step behind: we still hold only about 29% of C-suite roles and make up fewer than one in five decision-makers at venture firms. Even 2025, a banner year for women-founded startups, tells a misleading story: nearly 41% of the almost $74 billion raised came from two megadeals. Most women founders saw very few of those investment dollars.If women are already underrepresented among leaders, investors, and founders, and now we’re adopting AI more slowly, the gap widens at the exact moment the next generation of business leaders and global decision-makers are being decided.

#5331. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5330. Your Press Page is Rotting. A Yearly Audit Is the Only Thing That Stops It.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The coverage on your press page is decaying on the same schedule, and a yearly audit is the only thing that stops it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A quarter of the web from the last decade has vanished, and two-thirds of links eventually die. The coverage on your press page is decaying on the same schedule, and a yearly audit is the only thing that stops it.

A client sent me their press page last spring with some pride. Fourteen logos, a decade of coverage, the kind of wall a sales team loves to point at. I clicked through every link while we were on the call. Roughly a third were dead, two more redirected to a publication’s homepage and one article had vanished when the magazine that ran it was sold.

Nobody had done anything wrong. The page simply had not been checked since it was built, and the web had moved on without telling anyone. At ESBO Ltd, the link building and brand mentions agency I run, re-checking the placements we deliver is part of the job, and even so we lose some every year. Coverage is an asset that depreciates, and almost no company books the depreciation.

The scale is documented. When Pew Research Center sampled webpages that existed at any point between 2013 and 2023, 25% were no longer accessible by October 2023. Of pages that existed in 2013, 38% were gone. Nearly a quarter of news webpages contained at least one broken link, and the news sample was not obscure blogs but 2,063 sites a measurement company had classified as news.

Links die faster than pages. Ahrefs tracked links pointing at more than 2 million websites since 2013 and found 66.5% of them had rotted. Almost half of the lost links were dropped because the page or domain carrying them disappeared, and a third were removed by someone editing a page that still exists. Put those two causes together and your coverage is being deleted both by neglect and on purpose.

The causes are rarely dramatic. Publications fold or get sold, and the buyer prunes an archive it never wanted. A redesign migrates the site to a new content system and old addresses stop resolving. An editor runs a cleanup and strips outbound links from older articles, which is the 34% in the Ahrefs data and the one that stings most, because the article survives while your name’s connection to it does not.

Then there is the fine print. Some publishers sell placements with an expiry buried in the terms, and the article comes down on schedule 12 months later. I have written here before about four-figure placements vanishing overnight, but the slow version is more common and nobody notices it, because nobody is looking.

Three things go at once. The search value of the link disappears with the page. The social proof disappears from your press page, replaced by a logo that leads to an error, which is a worse impression on a buyer than no logo at all. And the mention falls out of the layer of the web that AI assistants read live. A system answering a question today can only cite pages that still resolve, so a dead article stops feeding the answer, even if an older training run remembers the name. Everything the mention was doing for you stops on a date nobody told you.

My own trade does not come out of this well. An agency that sells placements and never re-checks them is selling an asset with an unknown lifespan, and clients should ask about it far more often than they do.

Start by listing every address where your brand appears: the press page, old coverage reports, campaign spreadsheets, the links in your email signatures and investor decks. Most companies have never had that list in one place, and building it is half the value.

Run the list through any broken link checker, then sort the results into four piles. Dead domains, where the publication itself is gone. Dead pages on live sites, where the article was removed or moved. Removed links, where the article stands but no longer connects to you. And redirects, which usually mean a migration that lost your page along the way.

Each pile gets a different response. For a dead page on a live site, pull the copy from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, send it to the editor and ask whether the article can be restored or the reference updated; the hit rate is better than you would expect, because editors dislike broken archives too. For a removed link, ask once and politely, then let it go. For a dead domain, retire the logo from your press page and replace it with coverage that still loads. And for redirects, test whether the new address carries the mention, because sometimes it does and the fix is a copy and paste.

Then change how you acquire coverage so the next audit is shorter. Save an archived copy of every new article the day it appears. Before paying any publisher, ask in writing whether the placement is permanent, and treat a vague answer as a no. Put a yearly reminder in the calendar, because this work gets done only when it has a date.

Finally, spend on maintenance before you spend on growth. Restoring a mention that already exists costs one email, while earning a new one costs weeks. The press page that impresses a buyer in 2027 will not be the one with the most logos. It will be the one where every logo still goes somewhere, and that is a choice the company makes once a year, with a link checker and an afternoon.

A quarter of the web from the last decade has vanished, and two-thirds of links eventually die. The coverage on your press page is decaying on the same schedule, and a yearly audit is the only thing that stops it.

A client sent me their press page last spring with some pride. Fourteen logos, a decade of coverage, the kind of wall a sales team loves to point at. I clicked through every link while we were on the call. Roughly a third were dead, two more redirected to a publication’s homepage and one article had vanished when the magazine that ran it was sold.

Nobody had done anything wrong. The page simply had not been checked since it was built, and the web had moved on without telling anyone. At ESBO Ltd, the link building and brand mentions agency I run, re-checking the placements we deliver is part of the job, and even so we lose some every year. Coverage is an asset that depreciates, and almost no company books the depreciation.

#5329. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5328. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5327. The 10 Best Business Books to Put On Your Reading List in 2027

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Read these bestselling business books to hone your leadership skills.

Maybe you have a business idea in your Notes app that you keep thinking about. Or you could be trying to grow a company without letting it take over your life.

Whatever your next challenge looks like, there is something reassuring about learning from authors who have been exactly where you are or conducted research to help you grow.

The best business books show that success is found in the habits people repeat, the conversations they avoid and the attention they give each other.

These books help leaders notice those pivotal moments and make better decisions.

These 10 bestselling books approach business from different directions. Some focus on personal discipline, while others examine trust and creativity. Some were published in the early 20th century, while others debuted last month. They all offer ways to think more clearly about leadership.

James Clear’s Atomic Habits explains how habits develop and how to redesign routines so good behavior becomes easier. The four rules are to make it obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying. Systems matter more than goals, and repeated actions shape how we see ourselves. For business readers, this is a practical guide to turning ambition into routines. This book has sold more than 30 million copies since its debut nearly a decade ago.

This book, written by Will Guidara, is the story of how exceptional hospitality helped transform Eleven Madison Park into a celebrated restaurant over the course of 11 years. It shows that there is a difference between delivering competent service and making customers feel genuine care. The book describes memorable gestures and close attention to detail in customer interactions. It also showcases a workplace where employees can take initiative and leaders can encourage ownership. The book has sold more than a million copies.

In this book, David Epstein examines how limits can encourage experimentation and help people solve difficult problems. It draws on research and stories to explore when deadlines, scarce resources and careful boundaries support creativity instead of suppressing it. The question is if constraints help with the task at hand. This is a different way to approach innovation, through clearer boundaries instead of greater resources.

This book was written by former Navy SEAL officers Jocko Willink and Leif Babin, who translate combat leadership lessons into principles for business and everyday work. They say that leaders must take responsibility for their team’s results and not pin the blame on circumstances or other people. This means owning up to mistakes and explaining the mission clearly. They also have to develop a plan to improve. The biggest takeaway is that accountability begins with the leader’s own behavior.

Ever wanted to learn about leadership through the lives of great presidents? Doris Kearns Goodwin examines leadership through the examples of Abraham Lincoln, Theodore Roosevelt, Franklin Roosevelt and Lyndon Johnson and considers how experience and adversity shaped these presidents. The different crises they went through reveal different ways of responding to uncertainty. The book demonstrates how leaders can adapt when no playbook exists for the situations they are experiencing.

What do organizations lose when employees feel unable to speak honestly? They may notice a problem, have a useful question or recognize a mistake, yet remain silent because speaking feels like a personally risky move. Author Amy C. Edmondson presents psychological safety as a prerequisite for learning and innovation. She argues that information cannot help an organization if people are afraid to share it. The challenge for leaders is to create an environment where concerns surface early and prompt productive discussions.

Author Adam Grant, who is an organizational psychologist and professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, challenges the tendency to judge people by their starting point. His central argument is that potential depends more on how someone develops and less on where they begin. That shift changes how leaders think about talent because current achievement does not tell the full story of an employee’s future contributions. The book encourages attention to growth rather than fixed assumptions about ability.

Economist Joseph Schumpeter, who is often called the “father of entrepreneurship” or the “father of creative destruction,” wrote this book in 1942. In it, he examines how capitalism develops and why it changes societies. The book explains creative destruction, or the notion that innovation replaces established products, businesses and industries rather than just improving them. This is a demanding work of economic and political thought and offers readers a broader understanding of economic disruption.

In this book, which debuted in October, author Christina Wing examines the conversations people avoid even when silence leads to serious consequences. Her subjects include money, retirement, succession, failure, politics and other sensitive issues. She draws on work with family businesses, boards and classrooms to show how fear and secrecy can weaken relationships and delay important decisions. The book offers cases, questions, strategies and scripts for approaching difficult discussions. Its aim is clear communication grounded in empathy and respect.

This recently released book also from author Adam Grant focuses on connection. Why do some relationships deepen while others remain distant? How can people build a stronger sense of belonging? Vibe challenges the idea that meaningful bonds require similar personalities or immediate chemistry. It notes that connections can develop through shared experiences and curiosity. Examples include astronauts learning to trust colleagues they do not like and musicians strengthening relationships through disagreement. The book encourages a more deliberate approach to relationships. People can actively cultivate belonging.

Whatever your next challenge looks like, there is something reassuring about learning from authors who have been exactly where you are or conducted research to help you grow.
